articles.title_orig: Trump tells U.N. he could ‘annihilate’ Iran but expects a deal after the midterm elections
articles.title_zh: Trump tells U.N. he could ‘annihilate’ Iran but expects a deal after the midterm elections
articles.content_orig:
In a speech to world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly, President Donald Trump defended the Iran conflict and said he was considering whether to “annihilate” the country and drive it “into hell.”
Or, he said, Iran could make a deal with the U.S. that would allow the nation to rebuild. But that won’t happen until after the midterm elections in November, Trump predicted.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”
Trump later said U.S. envoys met with Iranian officials for three hours on the sidelines of the gathering, an unexpected development that offered a glimpse of diplomatic activity.
But Trump has repeatedly floated new attacks on Iran, even previously threatening death to the entire civilization . On Tuesday, he revived that warning at one of the most prominent platforms for world leaders, with an Iranian delegation in the audience.
“I have a big decision to make,” he said. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he continued.
Most important, Trump said to applause, is ensuring that “Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”
Iran’s nuclear potential was “the reality we had to confront,” he argued, and “a reality that far too many preferred to ignore.” Tehran has insisted its nuclear program is for civilian purposes and denied having plans to develop nuclear weapons.
The U.N. assembly comes as the Iran war is about to enter its eighth month.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the U.N. on Wednesday. Trump told Fox News that he would “probably” be open to meeting with Pezeshkian but did not announce any specifics.
Trump also highlighted peace deals he has worked on, U.S. actions in the Western Hemisphere and progress on his 20-point peace plan in the Gaza Strip.
Trump’s remarks to the assembly this year come as the U.N.’s Human Rights Council found in a report last week “reasonable grounds to believe” that the U.S. had committed war crimes during “indiscriminate attacks” against an Iranian school and a residential area in February.
The American president traditionally addresses the General Assembly each year.
During his wide-ranging speech, the president said America is “doing better than ever before,” touting the U.S. economy and his approach to immigration and artificial intelligence.
Less than a minute into his remarks, Trump called the U.S. economy “the envy of the world” and pointed to his administration’s tax policy and stock market records.
“Our economy is the envy of the world,” he said. “Our military is the most powerful on Earth. Our technology is second to none, and we are leading in virtually everything.”
Many American voters, though, don’t appear to agree. An NBC News poll conducted in September found that 56% of registered voters disapprove of the job the president is doing, and 55% said they believe his policies hurt the economy.
Gas prices remain high, sitting at an average of $4.47 per gallon, about a 50% increase since the war with Iran began. Diesel prices also spiked , affected by the Iran war as well as the war between Russia and Ukraine. Diesel hit a record $6 per gallon earlier this month before surging higher to $6.52 as of Tuesday, according to AAA .
Later, the president touted his record on immigration, tying his crackdown on the southern border to a drop in violent crime in the U.S.
“The entire world is being lifted by the wealth, strength, spirit and momentum of a newly energized and a very powerful United States of America,” he said.
While Trump declined to endorse guardrails on artificial intelligence, he did push for one change: its name.
Trump said the U.S. would refer in official documents to “superintelligence,” rather than “artificial intelligence.” The word “artificial,” Trump argued, “makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It’s actually amazing.”
Earlier this month, industry insiders warned that artificial intelligence could lead to human extinction, potentially in the next decade.
Trump said Tuesday that he would not “stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution.”
“We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in,” he said. “We’re going to watch it closely through the Department of Justice.”
Trump has previously said that the only guardrail the U.S. needs is “a STRONG AND SMART” president.
Artificial intelligence is also expected to be a main topic of conversation during Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week.
Trump met with several world leaders on the sidelines of the U.N. gathering, including Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez. It was Rodríguez’s first meeting with Trump since the U.S. captured then-Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, who are in a Brooklyn, New York, jail, awaiting trial.
Weeks ago, Trump said that the U.S. entered an agreement with Venezuela for U.S. majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of oil reserves in Venezuela.
On Tuesday, Trump called it “perhaps the biggest deal ever made,” adding: “To the victor belong the spoils.”
Trump said the Venezuela raid was “proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere,” noting U.S. attacks on drug cartels before pivoting to Cuba.
“My administration is seeking a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba,” he said, adding, “It will fall.”
In response, the Cuban delegation stood up and left the assembly hall.
Later Tuesday, Trump met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said: “I hope that we will end this war, and President Trump will help us help us end this war,” Zelenskyy said.
Trump said during his speech that the war in Ukraine would end “more quickly than people understand.”
For years, the president said he would end the war. During his 2024 presidential campaign , he said he could end the war within 24 hours or even before his presidency began.
Last week, Trump signed into law a Russian sanctions bill championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C.
He also announced that the U.S. would take over military operations and have “permanent control over security” in Greenland, in a deal signed later Tuesday with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark to try to end the tense standoff over the strategic Arctic territory.
Megan Brand is a politics reporter for NBC News.
Tara Prindiville is a White House producer for NBC News.
Abigail Williams is a producer and reporter for NBC News covering the State Department.
Raquel Coronell Uribe is a politics reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: How Ukraine’s devastating attacks on Putin’s oil refineries brought the war to Russia’s doorstep
articles.title_zh: How Ukraine’s devastating attacks on Putin’s oil refineries brought the war to Russia’s doorstep
articles.content_orig:

O n Sunday, just as polling closed in Russia ’s parliamentary elections, Ukraine launched one of its biggest drone strikes on Moscow since the war broke out over four years ago.
Striking images from the city showed a large refinery in flames and vast plumes of smoke billowing from chimneys . Over 450 drones were shot down in what the region’s mayor Sergei Sobyanin called “the most massive” attack it had seen.
The attacks came shortly after US president Donald Trump had ordered both sides to quit their attacks on energy infrastructure. But both countries have continued to attack each other despite the pleas.
According to a report by the International Energy Association , all but five of Russia’s 32 major oil refineries have escaped attack since war broke out, while some have been hit up to 15 times.
Those unaffected currently lie outside of the reach of Ukraine’s most advanced drones, between 3,500km and 6,500km from the border in eastern Siberia or the far east of the country.
The IEA has said that this strategy has intensified significantly over the past 18 months so that by June, throughput fell to its lowest level in more than 20 years and 30 per cent blow a year earlier.
Gasoline output has dropped by 20 per cent compared to 2024, while diesel production has fallen by nearly 30 per cent.
The attacks have led to images being released from Russia that will be unnerving for Russian leader Vladimir Putin : huge queues at fuelling stations (lasting up to 40 hours, according to some motorists), and rising oil and gas prices.
Fuel shortages have been reported across 92 per cent of Russia’s regions with around two-third introducing fuel-rationing measures.
The crisis has forced the Russian government to restrict oil exports to protect domestic supplies.
Ukraine’s military suggests that Russia’s total oil refining capacity is down by 45 per cent, according to a report by the General Staff released on Monday.
“Ukraine is increasingly using multiple waves of drones against individual refineries, seeking to overwhelm protective netting and other largely passive drone defence measures,” wrote the IEA.
“Its long-range capabilities and targeting have also advanced rapidly, particularly during the first half of 2026. This expanded reach enabled the 7 July strike on Gazprom Neft’s 450 thousand barrels per day (kb/d) Omsk refinery, Russia’s largest, roughly 2,500 kilometres from the Ukrainian border.”
The IEA says that there has not been “significant damage” reported to both primary and secondary crude oil processing units across the country.
As Ukraine becomes effective at striking the refineries it is “increasingly targeting specific refinery units to maximise the impact of each strike”.
It explained that Kyiv targets crude distillation units (CDUs), where the crude is initially processed, as well as secondary units such as fluid catalytic crackers (FCCs), hydrocrackers, reformers and hydrotreaters.
While damage to CDUs can typically be repaired within a week or two, damage to the more complex secondary units can take six to eight months to fix on average.
Russia has been forced to deal with the crisis by rationing fuel and also allowing the production of lower quality energy, allowing higher-sulphur grades of gasoline to be produced for the first time since 2016.
In May, the Washington Post reported that more than 20 strikes on Russian oil infrastructure in 2026 had cost Moscow over $7bn.
The Ukrainians have hit almost all the major refineries in European Russia and the Urals at least once. They have also damaged the country’s largest refinery located in Omsk (Siberia),” says John Lough, head of foreign policy at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre (NEST).
“It’s very difficult to put a figure on the total losses incurred through damage to refineries, lost production and overall disruption. It’s probably around $20 billion.”
But the picture is more complex as analysis by Reuters in July found that Russia’s oil and gas revenue had increased 60 per cent compared to the year before due to the increase in global oil prices.
The loss of oil prices is also putting further pressure on global oil supplies already squeezed due to the ongoing war in Iran , which has seen the Strait of Hormuz largely shut since March.
Whether the strategy has been effective in the long-run therefore may depend on multiple factors.
But Lough says that “its main value is psychological since it has brought the war home to Russians who were previously insulated from it and made them think about why the country is so poorly defended when the war was supposed to improve Russia’s security.”
“It’s hardly a coincidence that the authorities had to remove the Yabloko party from last weekend’s Duma elections. It was the only party campaigning for ending the war against Ukraine,” he added.
“It was supposed to receive only a tiny proportion of the vote, but the authorities concluded that its message risked resonating among the electorate.
“For Ukraine, it has been a double-edged sword. Russia has stepped up its own air campaign and has stopped the operation of the Black Sea ports – a lifeline for the Ukrainian economy. It has also intensified its attacks on other economic assets across the country.”

articles.title_orig: Trump administration to remove 760,000 Affordable Care Act enrollees over fraud claims
articles.title_zh: Trump administration to remove 760,000 Affordable Care Act enrollees over fraud claims
articles.content_orig:
Vice President JD Vance in the South Court Auditorium in the Eisenhower Executive Office Building on the White House campus, Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026, in Washington. Alex Brandon/AP hide caption
WASHINGTON — Vice President JD Vance and other Trump administration officials said Tuesday they plan to remove 760,000 Affordable Care Act enrollees from public healthcare exchanges, alleging that the individuals were fraudulently enrolled in the program, or simply do not exist.
Vance said the discovery and canceled subsidy payments for hundreds of thousands of people from the exchanges, part of an administration-wide crackdown on fraud, would result in $2.2 billion in cost savings.
"We're actually making sure that the people receiving Obamacare subsidies are actually entitled to receive them," said Vance, who leads a government task force to eliminate fraud. He was flanked by Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, or CMS, and other administration officials.
Vance said the cancellation of approximately 315,000 enrollments covering 760,000 people was done in part because the government was not checking whether people enrolled were eligible. Vance said another 419,000 enrollments will get additional verification to make sure they are eligible for the benefit.
The Trump administration also announced a six-month suspension on new agents or brokers who sign up enrollees for healthcare coverage, who officials say commit a disproportionate amount of the fraud they uncovered.
Roughly 19.2 million Americans are actively enrolled in ACA marketplace health plans as of early 2026, according to the Department of Health and Human Services website. The number of enrollees grew during the COVID-19 pandemic when enhanced subsidies became available through the American Rescue Plan Act and Inflation Reduction Act, both signed into law by former President Joe Biden.
Tuesday's announcement is the latest in an initiative by the Trump administration to address fraud around the country, including in federal healthcare programs, which officials say is needed to rein in runaway spending and protect taxpayers.
Some healthcare policy experts are calling for more transparency on how the Trump administration decided to cut hundreds of thousands of enrollees — and question how many people may have been wrongly cut from the program.
Cynthia Cox, a vice president and director of the ACA program at the healthcare research nonprofit KFF, said "I think there's no question that somebody who was fraudulently enrolled should have their coverage canceled," however, "I think the question is whether this was the appropriate process by which to identify fraudulent enrollees, and also whether all of them were indeed fraudulently enrolled."
Cox said the elimination of the people from ACA programs was done outside of the normal regulatory process.
Ellen Montz, a former deputy administrator and director at the Center for Consumer Information and Insurance Oversight at CMS during the Biden administration said during her time in government, there was an ongoing effort to eliminate fraud from ACA programs.
"There's a lot of work to be done, and the Trump administration has done some good things that are targeting the actual fraudsters," she said. Adding that Tuesday's announcement lacked details on how the administration determined who to cut. " I would imagine we'll hear from some subset of consumers that ask: why did my enrollment get cancelled?" Montz said.
At the press conference, Tuesday, Vance referred to some enrollments lacking social security numbers or immigration documentation.
The announcement comes as stubbornly high inflation and rising healthcare costs pressure the Trump administration to come up with a plan to bring down costs for Americans as affordability remains a central issue in the fall midterm elections.
The price of ACA insurance has skyrocketed for many Americans during Trump's second term, after Republicans opposed extending COVID-era subsidies that had helped offset the costs of health insurance for most enrollees during Biden's term.
Premiums doubled or tripled for many enrollees, prompting millions to downgrade their plans or exit the program entirely after the Republican-led Congress allowed the subsidies to expire this year.
The Government Accountability Office suggests fraud risks in the advance premium tax credit do exist - however it's unclear at what scale. The GAO conducted covert testing using fictitious ACA applicants enrolled in 2024 and 2025. A report released in December showed that the federal marketplace approved subsidized coverage for almost all of the GAO's 24 fake enrollees.
The White House referred The Associated Press to the Vice President's team for additional comment on bigger plans to address healthcare affordability. The Vice President's office and CMS did not respond to Associated Press requests for comment.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the news of the Trump administration's plan to remove ACA enrollees from public exchanges.
Democratic lawmakers criticized the move to remove enrollees from ACA coverage.
Richard E. Neal, a Massachusetts Democrat and ranking member of the Ways and Means Committee, said "Republicans have already created the worst healthcare crisis ever, but every decision by the Trump Administration is designed to keep making it worse."
"As if making coverage harder to access through skyrocketing premiums and more red tape wasn't painful enough, they're doubling down to take it away entirely," Neal said.

articles.title_orig: White House Defends Trump’s Ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico in Court Filing
articles.title_zh: White House Defends Trump’s Ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico in Court Filing
articles.content_orig:
Washington — CNN, MS NOW and Politico announced Monday that the news organizations are suing the Trump administration over President Trump's ban of the news outlets from the White House, arguing the ban was unconstitutional on First Amendment grounds.
Mr. Trump said Friday in a Truth Social post that he was barring CNN, MS Now, and Politico from the White House , in the Trump administration's latest move to target news outlets for what he views as disfavorable coverage.
In a joint statement on Monday, the three news organizations said they are suing to immediately restore access after they were denied entry on Saturday and had their press passes revoked.
"There could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment," the legal motion from the news organizations said. "Presidents from the earliest days of the Republic have disagreed with and complained about the tenor and content of press coverage of their administrations."
Mr. Trump posted on social media on Monday morning that the White House "is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America." He also wrote in a separate social media post, "FAKE NEWS IS A THREAT TO DEMOCRACY, and I will do whatever is necessary to make sure that the U.S.A. thrives."
The case was assigned to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed to the federal bench by Mr. Trump during his first term. Kelly oversaw a lawsuit brought by former CNN reporter Jim Acosta during the first Trump administration after the White House moved to revoke his access. The judge sided with Acosta after CNN sued and ordered his press pass to be restored, finding Acosta's due process rights under the Fifth Amendment had been violated. The White House obeyed the order.
Kelly scheduled a hearing on the CNN/MS NOW/Politico suit for Wednesday afternoon, and the Justice Department replied late Tuesday to the suit , saying the ban was at least partly on national security grounds.
The department argued that Kelly should deny the news organizations' motion to restore their access to the White House because "the President concluded that they have failed to maintain basic minimum 'standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including' by 'publishing sensitive or classified information.' ... In response, the president has preliminarily revoked their continued access to White House grounds. ... After all, access to the White House is a privilege — not a right."
The Trump administration, the DOJ said, is giving the outlets until Sept. 25 at 5 p.m. to contest the decision to revoke access.
The lawsuit is asking a Washington, D.C., judge to move quickly to prevent further action from the White House on the ban. CNN was scheduled to be traveling with the president on Monday as the network pool team. Without a replacement, there was no television network traveling with Mr. Trump — an unprecedented move.
The motion says they have notified the Trump administration of their intent to sue. The lawsuit names Mr. Trump and three of his top aides — Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, as well as spokesperson Steven Cheung and Secret Secret chief Sean Curran.
Speaking to reporters after the announcement on Friday, Mr. Trump said there is "no reason" why the ban was issued when it was, and suggested it wasn't in response to any specific incident.
"I don't think somebody should be allowed to come and write fake stories. They're fake news. And they have no credibility," Mr. Trump said. "Now, if they want to write them, that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my —  into the people's house."
Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press President Bruce Brown called the ban "flatly unconstitutional." He said the decision to block the outlets from White House grounds was "textbook viewpoint discrimination and will be quickly struck down by the courts if challenged."
The administration curbed news outlets' access to the Pentagon last year. The Defense Department required journalists with daily access to the building to sign onto a slew of rules, including one that suggested reporters who "solicit" sensitive information could be deemed a security risk and kicked out of the Pentagon. Most news outlets — including CBS News, ABC News, NBC News, Fox News and CNN — declined to sign and left the Pentagon.
After a judge struck down some of those rules earlier this year, the Defense Department changed course and began requiring any reporters on Pentagon grounds to be escorted by government personnel. An appeals court allowed that policy to remain in place .
In its response to the CNN/MS NOW/Politico suit late Tuesday, the DOJ included two sworn statements, one from Kingsley Lewis, the Pentagon press secretary, and the other from a top Pentagon official, claiming that after the Pentagon limited media access, leaks have slowed, and the same would happen if the White House ban is allowed to proceed.
The Trump administration has made other attempts to remove media outlets from the White House and other spaces.
Last year, Mr. Trump barred The Associated Press from attending certain White House events after the news outlet refused to conform to Mr. Trump's proclamation that the Gulf of Mexico was now the "Gulf of America."
The wire service sued on First Amendment grounds shortly afterwards, and while a federal judge in D.C. initially ruled that the White House must restore the news outlet's access, an appeals court later allowed the ban to take effect .
The appellate ruling hinged on the fact that the AP was blocked from certain restricted spaces like the Oval Office and Air Force One that only a small subset of the White House press corps can access — a narrower policy than the outright ban imposed on CNN, MS NOW and Politico. The appeals court judges said the White House can't ban journalists from spaces that are "generally open to the press," like the briefing room, based on their viewpoint.
As the legal process played out, the White House assumed control of the press pool, a small, rotating group of journalists who cover the president every day and disseminate information and footage to other news outlets. The print press pool works in rotation so that wire outlets, including the AP, are now not granted access to spaces like Air Force One or the Oval Office as frequently as they once were.
Kathryn  Watson contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: Discord’s age verification era is upon us, despite community backlash
articles.content_orig:

Starting Wednesday, Discord, the community messaging platform, will roll out age verification measures to all users.
The rollout comes after the company initially delayed its age verification plans in February due to backlash from users concerned that biometric scans and ID checks could jeopardize their privacy . Those concerns weren’t unfounded; last year, a third-party vendor that works with Discord was breached , potentially exposing the data of 70,000 users’ data, including government ID photos and selfies used for identity verification.
“Age assurance draws strong opinions and skepticism, especially when it involves sharing biometric information or a form of ID,” Discord CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy wrote in a blog post , published Tuesday. “At the same time, age assurance laws are expanding, and since my last post we’ve had to launch age assurance in other regions, including in Brazil and in Texas.”
However, Vishnevskiy says more than 90% of Discord users won’t have to verify their age. He explains that Discord will instead use existing account data to detect “signals,” like account tenure (how long an account has existed), device and activity data, and other usage patterns, to determine whether a user belongs in the adult, teen, or unconfirmed age group.
Discord says that it doesn’t estimate users’ ages based on message content, profile data, or demographic attributes.
“The way a typical 15-year-old uses Discord (including how many communities they’re a part of and how they interact with others) looks different in aggregate from how a typical 30-year-old uses Discord,” the company wrote in a separate, technical blog post, also published Tuesday. “Our [machine learning] model has learned these patterns to predict whether a given account likely belongs to an adult or a teen.”
This doesn’t mean that Discord is collecting new user data. It’s standard for social media companies to retain this kind of data on their customers, even though it might feel unsettling to see it spelled out so overtly.
Because local laws have required Discord to use age assurance technology in certain regions due to local law, the company was able to train its model on reliably confirmed data linking user behavior to age.
If Discord is not confident that a user is an adult, that user can still prove their age without a biometric or ID scan. They can appeal by sharing a credit card or age group data from their Apple App Store or Google Play Store account.
For confirmed adults, nothing about the platform will change. Teens accounts, however, will automatically be blocked from accessing age-restricted servers or channels. Message requests from people who aren’t their friends will go to a separate message requests inbox, and teens will get alerts when accepting friend requests from someone they don’t share mutual friends with.
As governments around the world continue passing age verification requirements in an attempt to protect children online, experts warn that these age checks can create a host of new privacy and security issues. That leaves platforms like Discord with a difficult choice: comply or risk sanctions.

articles.title_orig: New Mac Mini Has Two Storage Downsides, Including Unremovable SSD
articles.title_zh: New Mac Mini Has Two Storage Downsides, Including Unremovable SSD
articles.content_orig:
As confirmed by the website "Expand Mac mini," NAND storage in the new Mac mini models with the M6 and M5 Pro chips is soldered to the logic board, whereas the previous models with the M4 and M4 Pro chips have removable storage that can be upgraded.
In other words, the new Mac mini does not support aftermarket storage upgrades.
"Expand Mac mini" offers plug-and-play SSD modules that are functionally equivalent to Apple's proprietary modules, yet hundreds of dollars cheaper. As a result, customers were able to save a significant amount of money by configuring their Mac mini with the minimum 256GB capacity that was available on Apple's online store and later installing a higher-capacity aftermarket module. With the new models, that is no longer possible.
"We will keep looking for an opening, but support for the M6 and M5 Pro now looks unlikely," the "Expand Mac mini" website said, in a blog post.
Mac mini models with the M1 chip and M2/M2 Pro chips also had NAND soldered to the logic board, so the M4/M4 Pro configurations having removable storage has proven to be a one-off exception for now. Apple has not commented on the reversal.
In addition, all new Mac mini configurations with 256GB of storage reportedly have a single NAND chip, rather than a pair of 128GB chips. As a result, 256GB configurations have slower SSD speeds compared to configurations with 512GB of storage or more that do have dual NAND chips, according to AAPL Ch. 's testing with Blackmagic's Disk Speed Test benchmark tool.
The new 256GB model's Disk Speed Test scores were roughly half that of models with 512GB of storage or more. The average customer is unlikely to notice the difference, but power users will appreciate knowing that they need to opt for at least 512GB of storage in order to achieve the fastest SSD speeds possible.
Fortunately, even with 256GB of storage, it appears that the new Mac mini has meaningfully faster SSD speeds compared to the previous 256GB model.
Mac mini models with M2/M2 Pro and 256GB of storage also had a single NAND chip , so the M4/M4 Pro configurations proved to be a one-off exception for this too.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he backs diesel export ban to curb soaring energy costs
articles.title_zh: 特朗普表示，他支持柴油出口禁令，以遏制能源成本飙升
articles.summary_zh: 唐纳德·特朗普周二表示，他支持禁止柴油出口的想法，一些美国政客呼吁这是遏制能源成本飙升的一种方式。
articles.content_orig:
But industry trade group says plan would backfire and lead to even higher prices for gasoline
US politics live – latest updates
Donald Trump on Tuesday said he backed ⁠the idea of a ban on diesel exports, which some US politicians are calling for ⁠as a way ⁠to curb ​the soaring cost of energy.
Diesel prices have rallied in Europe and the US to ⁠record highs as wars in Iran and Ukraine sharply cut exports from some of the biggest producers ⁠such as Russia, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. A gallon of diesel fuel in the US was $6.53 on Tuesday, the highest average on record and over 75% higher than a year ago.
“I’ve ​said let’s not send ‌out the diesel. ‌We make a lot of diesel … I’ve called for it. ‌I’ve called for it within my people,” Trump told reporters ahead of a meeting with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, speaking at the same meeting, said: “We’re examining whether it’s feasible in terms of the overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work.”
On Sunday, Trump urged Zelenskyy to pause strikes on Russian oil refineries over concerns that they could further push up prices, the Financial Times reported . On social media, Trump wrote that Russia “unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry”.
Some Republican Senate candidates in the most ​competitive midterm races called for the administration to implement the export ban to try to alleviate high costs for Americans.
“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” wrote the US representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican who is in a competitive Senate race in Iowa, on X . “We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices.”
In a statement, the American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers trade group said that an export ban would “backfire”, noting that domestic refiners would have to reduce production and “producing less diesel also means producing less gasoline”.
Trump said he and Zelenskiy would ⁠discuss Ukrainian attacks on refining sites in Russia .
“It is ​a serious ​hit on the Russians. ​It’s also a serious hit on the price ​of diesel,” said ‌Trump, who ​also told ​reporters the two leaders would discuss working out a solution to end Russia’s war in Ukraine .
“I think it’s going to happen,” Trump said, of a potential solution to the war.
Reuters contributed reporting
articles.content_zh:
唐纳德·特朗普周二表示，他支持禁止柴油出口的想法，一些美国政客呼吁这是遏制能源成本飙升的一种方式。
欧洲和美国的柴油价格上涨至历史新高，因为伊朗和乌克兰的战争大幅削减了俄罗斯、沙特阿拉伯和阿拉伯联合酋长国等一些最大生产国的出口。周二，美国一加仑柴油的价格为6.53美元，创历史新高，比一年前上涨了75%以上。
特朗普在与乌克兰总统弗拉基米尔·泽连斯基会晤前告诉记者：“我说过，我们不要发送柴油。我们生产了很多柴油……我呼吁这样做。我在我的人民中呼吁这样做”。
美国财政部长Scott Bessent在同一次会议上表示：“我们正在研究从整体炼油能力来看是否可行，以及全面或部分禁令是否可行。”
据英国《金融时报》报道，周日，特朗普敦促泽连斯基暂停对俄罗斯炼油厂的罢工，因为担心炼油厂可能会进一步推高油价。特朗普在社交媒体上写道，俄罗斯“不幸失去了对柴油工业的控制”。
在竞争最激烈的中期选举中，一些共和党参议院候选人呼吁政府实施出口禁令，以减轻美国人的高昂成本。
“爱荷华州人正在受到挤压，不应该在加油站或伊朗战争的结账线上买单，”美国众议员阿什利·欣森在X上写道。“我们需要利用我们掌握的每一种选择来缓解高昂的价格。”欣森是一名共和党人，正在爱荷华州参加竞争激烈的参议院竞选
美国燃料和石化制造商贸易组织在一份声明中表示，出口禁令将“适得其反”，并指出国内炼油厂将不得不减产，“减少柴油产量也意味着减少汽油产量”。
特朗普表示，他和泽连斯基将讨论乌克兰对俄罗斯炼油厂的袭击。
特朗普表示：“这对俄罗斯人来说是一个严重打击。这也对柴油价格造成了严重打击。”他还告诉记者，两位领导人将讨论制定一个解决方案来结束俄罗斯在乌克兰的战争。
“我认为这将会发生，”特朗普在谈到战争的潜在解决方案时说。

articles.title_orig: Report: Jaxson Dart’s injury could be season-ending
articles.title_zh: Report: Jaxson Dart’s injury could be season-ending
articles.content_orig:
One day after an apparently serious injury to Bears starting quarterback Caleb Williams ended up being not nearly as bad as it seemed, an injury to Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart has turned out to be far worse than believed.
Via NFL Network, an MRI showed that Dart’s knee injury is worse than expected. He’s now expected to be out an extended period of time, and possibly for the rest of the season.
It’s very bad news for a team that showed great promise in Week 1, and it moves Jameis Winston into the starting job. He struggled in relief of Dart on Monday night, completing 11 of 27 passes for 111 yards and an interception.
The Giants have no other quarterbacks on the 53-man roster; Jake Haener is on the practice squad. Which means that the Giants will likely be scouring all available options for another player at the position — from free agency to a potential trade with a team that has a surplus at the position.
Originally, it was believed that Dart had an MCL sprain. Coach John Harbaugh told reporters on Monday night that the injury was in that “neighborhood.” Clearly, it wasn’t.

articles.title_orig: Burnham passes his first Trump test — but papers over the cracks
articles.title_zh: Burnham passes his first Trump test — but papers over the cracks
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK — Before Andy Burnham’s meeting with Donald Trump, a senior U.K. government figure noted wryly that they were looking out for one thing — whether the U.S. president would claim that Burnham was better than the last guy.
After nearly an hour together in a cramped, low-ceilinged room in the United Nations basement, Trump did exactly that.
The president said U.K.-U.S. relations were “more up now than they were with your last prime minister.” Moments later he put the boot into Keir Starmer again, claiming the ex-PM’s tough rhetoric on Russia had been “too tough.”
That final comment will please Starmer, who welcomed Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Britain after Trump berated him in the Oval Office. But it also shows how far his relationship with Trump fell after his initial attempts to please the president in early 2025.
Burnham had the benefit of a fresh start, and ahead of his first meeting with Trump, British officials insisted he would take a less fawning approach than his predecessor. He could afford to do so, they said, because Trump’s presidency is almost at the midway point and there is less to lose.
Yet there were similarities to Starmer’s early days. Both leaders were on their best behavior, straining not to upset each other in public.
They each gave the other a free pass. Burnham sat expressionless as Trump talked about “fake news” media, while Trump did the same as Burnham talked about Britain’s recent sanctions on West Bank settlements.
Burnham raised the salience of immigration, an issue Trump invoked against Starmer, while Trump even praised Burnham’s “great election win.” (Burnham has not won a general election, merely a special election for the parliamentary seat of Makerfield.)
But some things were different. The splits between the two nations were closer to the surface than in Starmer’s first trip — and even in those cordial words for the cameras, the divides broke into the open.
Trump seized on a Daily Telegraph journalist’s invitation to condemn the long-stalled British plan to hand sovereignty of the Chagos Islands, a strategically vital archipelago in the Indian Ocean, to Mauritius. His words were little surprise on their own, but Burnham’s response — in which he repeatedly refused to rule out reopening the terms of the deal to satisfy Trump’s concerns — formed a genuine shift in U.K. policy.
It remains unclear how any deal could satisfy the demands of Mauritius and the U.S. at the same time.
Then there was the gulf between the two leaders on AI regulation.
Burnham used a breakfast Tuesday in New York with business figures, including Apple’s Tim Cook, to call for an agreed global set of standards on the technology.
Barely an hour later, Trump used his speech at the U.N. General Assembly rostrum to condemn “globalist” attempts to regulate what he called “super intelligence.”
Burnham spent almost an hour in a room with the leader of the free world (and an eight-strong delegation on each side), yet appears not to have raised AI with Trump at all. Downing Street repeatedly refused to say he brought it up and there was no mention of it the official readout.
After it was all over, Burnham used his speech to UNGA to put his appeal to domestic cost-of-living issues on a world stage.
He also announced a “national center for information defense” (with little detail) that would counter disinformation; he portrayed Britain as an “honest broker” on controlling AI. But Britain’s decision not to back a declaration by 22 countries on global AI controls earlier in the week meant it could be sidelined. (Burnham said Britain would look at multiple initiatives, including that one.)
There were other potential wrinkles. Burnham said he would speak in defense of the Falkland Islands, weeks after Trump gave fuel to Argentina’s long-standing claims on their sovereignty by suggesting he would not help if Argentina tried to invade.
Burnham also revealed that he made a plea to Trump about U.S. tariffs and their effect on a particular factory in the northeast of England (he would not say which one). Despite the carve-outs that Starmer won, British industry — especially the automobile sector — is still being hit by Trump’s tariffs.
But so much that could have gone wrong, didn’t — at least for now. Trump did not use the time before the cameras to bring up Britain’s difficult progress toward spending 3.5% of GDP on defense, and did not hit out over the pace of the decision to allow oil and gas drilling in the North Sea.
The newbie prime minister looked buttoned-up during the moment for the cameras with Trump, relaxing only when he was asked about Manchester, where he spent nine years as mayor. The world stage is still new to him.
And in that context, his aides will be chalking the first meeting up overall as a win — just as Starmer’s aides did on the way back from New York two years ago this week. Trump praised Burnham as a natural businessman, a man who “gets it.” The vibes, in this relatively easy opening period, were good.
He will need to maintain the influence if he can. Burnham later said he lobbied Trump to press for an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia. Pressure on the U.S. to release more air defense missiles to Ukraine ahead of the winter will only increase.
While Burnham didn’t invite him to the U.K. on Tuesday, they did pave the way for another visit to one of Trump’s golf resorts. “I said I was having second thoughts about playing golf with him, given a recent performance of my own was probably not up to the right standard,” Burnham told broadcasters.
For the man who wasn’t going to bend the knee to Trump, flattery will get him everywhere.

articles.content_orig:
[This story contains spoilers for episode three of Dancing With the Stars season 35.]
Dancing With the Stars paid homage to the hottest songs for Viral Hits Night.
Tuesday night, competing couples hit the ballroom to perform numbers inspired by “some of the biggest viral hits and unforgettable moments that have taken the internet by storm,” per ABC . It marks the third episode of season 35; however the second week of competition after last week’s special two-night premiere.
By the end of Viral Hits Night, Giada De Laurentiis and Alan Bersten were eliminated from DWTS season 35.
Celebrities still in the competition are Tatyana Ali, Tyler Cameron, Jenna Dewan, Ezra French, Amber Glenn, Taylor Hanson, Maura Higgins, Ciara Miller , Jackson Olson, Guillermo Rodriguez, Harry Shum Jr., Julia Stiles and Connor Wood.
Last Tuesday during the premiere, the male celebrities performed and Conner Leavitt was eliminated. Wednesday night, the women hit the ballroom , and Sarah Jane Nader became the second celebrity eliminated.
Jenna and Val Chmerkovskiy kicked off Viral Hits Night, cementing the early lead of 21/30 for their Jive to Katseye’s “Animal.” Ciara and Brandon Armstrong trailed closely behind, scoring an 18/30 after they performed a Tango to “No Broke Boys” by Disco Lines and Tinashe.
Ezra and Daniella Karagach went on to tie Jenna and Val’s score, earning three sevens from the judges. They performed a Cha Cha to Flo Rida’s “Low,” leaving the ballroom on their feet in applause.
After Tatyana and Jan Ravnik danced a Foxtrot to Billie Eilish’s “What Was I Made For?,” host Alfonso Ribeiro announced that Viral Hits Night had already received more fan votes than both premieres. However, just before the eliminated couple was announced, Alfonso announced that the number of votes triumphed over that of the season 34 DWTS finale.
Amber and Pasha Pashkov also emerged to tie the top leaderboard score (21/30) for their Tango to “All the Things She Said” by Harrison, an homage to Heated Rivalry , of course. That meant Jenna, Ezra and Amber tied for the top of the leaderboard; Maura trailed with a 19/30. Giada and Guillermo tied for the bottom of the leaderboard, each with a 12/30.
The couple with the lowest combined total of judges’ scores and viewer votes is eliminated at the end of each DWTS episode. Live voting takes place during the East Coast airing of each show and ends shortly after the final performance; that means if you’re a West Coast viewer and want to vote, you must do so between 5 p.m. PT and roughly 6:45 p.m. PT, as voting ends after the final performance.

articles.title_orig: New Adtech From Microsoft Would Interrupt Your Game at 'Promoted Content Trigger Events'
articles.title_zh: New Adtech From Microsoft Would Interrupt Your Game at 'Promoted Content Trigger Events'
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft already shows you ads whenever you log into the Xbox Series X , but it seems like it's exploring an ad-supported way to essentially rent out games on Xbox consoles.
Microsoft filed a patent called 'contextually aware management of interactive software application access,' which describes a process of pausing your game at the operating system level and presenting 'audiovisual promoted content' (in other words, an ad), which would then grant you a credit once it's over. That credit, at least in the way it's presented in the patent documentation, would grant you access to the game for a limited amount of time, from 15 minutes to an hour.
It's important to keep in mind that there's no way to tell whether or not the technology presented in this patent will ever get implemented. But, considering the troubles Xbox Game Pass has been dealing with lately , it's not that bizarre to imagine an ad-supported tier where you have to watch an ad every 15 minutes to keep playing your game.
Keep in mind that Microsoft also recently limited playtime on Xbox Cloud Gaming to just 15 hours a month with Game Pass Ultimate . That's not a lot of time to play games, and anyone relying on cloud streaming, now that RAM prices have gone through the roof, could be stuck dealing with the ads just to play games for more than 30 minutes a day.
Hopefully, if this patent does materialize into something real, it'll be a way to let people play for free, rather than being snuck into games that people paid full price for. However, even Disney+ looks like it's going to work ads into its most expensive subscription plan, so it's not off the table for Microsoft to do the same.
After all, this patent comes at a time when Microsoft is aggressively trying to make Xbox more profitable. The company just had another round of layoffs, where it handed Halo to Activision and got rid of a Halo Studios cinematic director the same week that he was promoted. Project Helix is also lurking around the corner, and it's probably going to be incredibly expensive, thanks to the ongoing RAM crisis .
Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title_orig: US criticises Australia's proposed algorithm opt-out laws as 'censorship'
articles.title_zh: US criticises Australia's proposed algorithm opt-out laws as 'censorship'
articles.content_orig:
The US has criticised Australia's proposal to give users the ability to opt out of social media algorithms, saying it amounts to "censorship of protected speech".
Under Australia's draft digital duty of care laws, tech firms risk hefty fines if they fail to give users the option to turn off algorithms in a bid to protect them from harmful content.
In a rare submission to the proposed laws, the US embassy in Canberra said it had "serious concerns" and allowing the government to "enforce vague definitions of 'harm'" would lead to "viewpoint-based censorship".
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the legislation was not about giving governments control but giving it back to individuals.
"We ask that Australia clarify how exactly 'harm' and 'risks' shall be determined... ensuring these definitions do not encroach on protected speech," the US said in its submission.
The US also claimed that the proposed laws may risk "reducing the reach of independent journalists or other voices whose content touches on sensitive or controversial topics" if tech firms had to "pre-emptively demote" them.
An opt-out option would "allow regulators to impose rigid, one-size-fits-all platform design requirements" on tech firms and this could affect users outside of Australia, it said.
"Mandated platform design features, especially when applied to algorithms, may affect what users see, say, and hear not just in or from Australia, but globally."
The US also called on Australia to address industry concerns that the "biases and preferences" of government officials do not "disadvantage independent or minority-viewpoint speech".
Another worry was that the proposed laws could affect Australia's "reputation as a jurisdiction that enables innovation," the submission said.
The criticism comes during Albanese's visit to the US to speak at the UN's General Assembly about his government's tech policies.
On Tuesday, local time in New York, Albanese responded to the criticism and claims of the proposed laws being government overreach.
"It's not about giving government control," he told the media in New York.
"It's about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices."
US President Donald Trump meanwhile used his speech at the UN to play down fears about AI, rejecting proposals for guardrails on it and arguing it should be renamed "super intelligence" as "the use of the word artificial makes it sound fake".
This latest move by Australia to protect its online users from harm comes less than a year after the country introduced a social media ban for children under 16 last December.

articles.title_orig: Trump berates CNN’s Kaitlan Collins after ban: ‘You shouldn’t be covering me’
articles.title_zh: 特朗普在禁令后斥责CNN的凯特兰·柯林斯：“你不应该报道我”
articles.summary_zh: 白宫媒体禁令后，特朗普在联合国与美国有线电视新闻网的凯特兰·柯林斯进行了紧张的交流：“你不应该在这里”
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump lashed out at a CNN journalist Tuesday morning at the United Nations , telling her, "You should not be here covering me," as the Department of Justice prepares to defend in federal court his ban on that media outlet, MS NOW and Politico from the White House.
CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins had asked Trump about a new poll that found two-thirds of Americans do not think the U.S. is winning its war with Iran .
"When will it end?" Collins asked the president.
"So it's an honor to be here. I'm surprised that CNN is here covering me," Trump told reporters as he gestured at Collins, before he entered the General Assembly in New York to address that body.
Collins interjected, "The United Nations allowed us in here, sir."
"You should not be here," Trump told Collins. "You should not be here covering me. You said you weren't going to cover me."
After Trump left, Collins later noted on air, "We never said we were never going to cover the president."
"We will continue to cover the president despite their efforts to block CNN from the White House grounds," she said.
Trump last Friday said he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, citing what he called false stories about him and his administration. Trump has frequently criticized news coverage of him and did not point to specific stories.
That ban took effect Saturday morning, when Secret Service officers at the White House took press passes from journalists from those three outlets when they arrived to work there.
On Monday, the three outlets filed a lawsuit against Trump in U.S. District Court in Washington, asking a judge to block the president's ban and restore their access to the White House. The suit alleges Trump violated the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution and the Constitution's Due Process Clause in summarily barring the outlets.
"We are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," the outlets said in a joint statement on Monday.
Also Monday, the five-member consortium of TV news networks that rotates pool coverage of the White House said four of those networks would suspend pool coverage ahead of Trump's trip to New York because the White House was not allowing CNN to act as the pool as was originally scheduled. It's not clear if that suspension will continue when Trump returns to Washington and another outlet is scheduled to act as the White House TV pool.
The consortium, which includes ABC News, CBS News, Fox News and NBC News, in addition to CNN, provides video of Trump events to other media outlets for their use.
The suspension of pool coverage does not change how CNN or the other networks separately cover Trump's visit to New York and the UN.
Kelly, the Trump-appointed judge assigned to handle the lawsuit challenging his media ban, has ordered the Department of Justice to respond to the outlets' request for an injunction against the ban on Tuesday.
Kelly scheduled a teleconference hearing on the request for Wednesday.
Trump told reporters on Tuesday that he expected Kelly to rule against him and asked whether he would let the outlets back into the White House if the judge ordered it.
"It probably will, because this is a judge who's not a particularly fair judge," Trump said of Kelly.
In November 2018, Kelly ordered the White House to restore the press pass of then-CNN correspondent Jim Acosta, whose credentials had been revoked after a contentious exchange with Trump.
MS NOW reported Tuesday that it had obtained talking points the White House had sent congressional Republicans about Trump's ban of the outlets. Talking points are designed to be used as a response to questions from journalists about a specific topic.
Among other things, the talking points say, "No president has been more transparent or offered more of his time to the press," and, "the First Amendment protects their right to publish; it does not entitle certain outlets and members of the press to a hard pass, briefing room seat, or place in the press pool." A "hard pass" is a long-term press credential for journalists who regularly cover the White House.
"Fabricating facts or reporting verifiable falsehoods from inside the White House complex is an intentional breach of professional decorum and it is severely disruptive to the mission and purpose of the White House," another talking point says.

白宫媒体禁令后，特朗普在联合国与美国有线电视新闻网的凯特兰·柯林斯进行了紧张的交流：“你不应该在这里”
在您的搜索结果中查看更多我们的报道。
在谷歌上添加《纽约邮报》
在全球舞台上进行高风险外交的一天，唐纳德·特朗普总统在访问联合国时对一位著名的美国记者说：“你不应该来这里。”
“很荣幸来到这里，”特朗普周二在联合国大会演讲前走进联合国大门时说，他面对的是美国有线电视新闻网的凯特兰·柯林斯，他经常成为他的愤怒目标。“我很惊讶CNN在这里报道我。你不应该在这里报道。你说过你不会报道我的。”
正如柯林斯后来在节目中指出的那样，美国有线电视新闻网没有说任何类似的话。几天前，政府禁止美国有线电视新闻网与NOW和Politico一起进入白宫，并取消了该网络的共享税。但美国有线电视新闻网已被联合国接纳为定期认证的媒体。
无论如何，这一紧张时刻清楚地提醒人们，特朗普与他反对其报道为“假新闻”的新闻机构之间的激烈冲突在短短几天内就急剧升级。
目前的禁令是这三家媒体周一提起的联合诉讼的主题，要求法官认定政府的举动违宪。白宫必须在周二之前作出回应，听证会定于周三下午举行。
特朗普表示，他有权“清除假新闻”
周二晚些时候，特朗普进一步强化了他的言论，并表示负面报道对国家来说是危险的。
当被问及如果法院做出不利于白宫的裁决，他是否会允许媒体重返白宫时，他说：“好吧，很可能会，因为这位法官不是一位特别公平的法官。”他指的是美国地区法官蒂莫西·凯利，他在2017年任命了他，并在2018年的一个类似案件中下令恢复CNN记者的访问权限。
“所以你永远不知道，”特朗普补充道。“我认为我们有权清除假新闻。”
特朗普的评论呼应了他自周五宣布禁令以来所做的其他评论。他提到了“故意负面报道”，但没有引用具体的报道——只是笼统地说是“假新闻”——作为禁令的理由。
这项禁令和诉讼是总统（尤其是在他的第二任期内）与他认为不利的媒体之间长期冲突的一部分。特朗普在法庭上做出了回应，或者采取了监管行动。他还亲自或多次抨击个别记者

articles.title_orig: President Trump’s money managers made more than 1,100 trades in July
articles.title_zh: President Trump’s money managers made more than 1,100 trades in July
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump's money managers made 1,152 trades on his behalf in July alone, according to his latest financial disclosure Tuesday — an astronomical number relative to his predecessors, and still high by the standard of active traders.
The transactions included many companies such as SpaceX and RTX (formerly known as Raytheon) that do business with the federal government, in industries his administration helps regulate.
The financial transactions amount to roughly 50 trades a day, a heavy volume for a typical investor but consistent with Trump's portfolio activity in his second term. According to a Bloomberg analysis , Trump or his managers have executed more than 28,000 trades since his second inauguration in January 2025 — more than every member of the House and Senate, combined.
Former presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama didn't trade individual stocks, as their portfolios relied primarily on mutual funds and US Treasuries.
The scale of the trading — which included as much as $25 million in sales of shares of both Microsoft and Amazon — has deepened concerns about the potential for corruption.
The amount of turnover "does seem high," even by the standards of a tactical investor trying to time the market, said Brett Bernstein, CEO and co-founder of XML Financial Group. But even if the "optics aren't always great," the volume alone doesn't necessarily indicate corruption.
"It depends on someone's approach to investing… if they have a tactical portfolio manager that's timing markets with strategies, it doesn't seem overly crazy," Bernstein added.
Trump declined to place his assets in a blind trust – meaning he has the ability to see which stocks his money managers are buying or selling. Trump's signature appears on his financial disclosure form listing all of his trades, indicating he has seen the document and is aware of at least some of his holdings.
"President Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions," Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, told CNN.
"All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000. Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers. There are no conflicts of interest," Ingle added.
Last month, a CNN investigation found that Trump has promoted more than 20 companies on his Truth Social account days after buying stock in those firms – at times announcing government actions that could benefit the companies he just invested in.
"Prior presidents did not engage in the stock market in this way," Donald Sherman, president of the nonpartisan ethics watchdog CREW, told CNN. "You have numerous examples of Republican and Democratic presidents who took steps to avoid conflicts of interest, and President Trump seems to be taking advantage of every opportunity to profit off of his government service."
CNN's Kit Maher contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Paramount-Warner Bros. Settlement to Be Considered at Thursday Court Hearing
articles.title_zh: Paramount-Warner Bros. Settlement to Be Considered at Thursday Court Hearing
articles.content_orig:
The federal judge overseeing the now-settled bid from a dozen states challenging Paramount ‘s $110 bid to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery will consider on Thursday whether to dissolve their joint agreement not to close the deal.
The purpose of the hearing is to “address certain outstanding questions regarding the factual and legal underpinnings of the parties’ proposed consent decree” and its implementation, according to a court document filed on Tuesday.
The hearing will follow a landmark settlement struck over the weekend to resolve the lawsuit, clearing the way for Hollywood’s next media and entertainment colossus. The deal doesn’t require any divestitures typical of enforcer-friendly deals. Instead, it appears to be a five-year operating agreement imposed through a consent decree.
Under the settlement, Paramount and Warner Bros. must release at least 30 theatrical films a year for the first two years and 32 for the following three, maintain minimum numbers of wide and independent releases and ensure that at least half of the films are produced or jointly produced by the combined company. Other notable terms: Keeping the studios’ basic-cable negotiations separate and the creation of a five-member independent board overseeing editorial standards at CBS News and CNN (selected by Paramount). A violation of the former term could see an order forcing the studio to divest from BET, VH1 and Comedy Central, among other channels (blue-chip assets like CNN or New Line Cinema are not on the table in these divestiture scenarios).
After the deal was reached, Paramount and California asked the court to enter into the consent decree, which would resolve the lawsuit. They moved for the court to lift an order issued in July barring Paramount from closing the deal.
U.S. District Judge U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin must still approve the agreement.
The court will have continued oversight of the combined company under the five-year consent decree. An independent monitor and small group of state attorneys general will oversee compliance. Paramount is required to provide information and reports necessary to assess whether it’s meeting the settlement’s terms, giving the states some visibility into the studio’s operations.
The arrangement also gives the court a mechanism to intervene if Paramount fails to live up to those commitments. The decree provides for enforcement proceedings and financial penalties for certain violations, with more serious breaches exposing the company to potential divestitures. One example: Violation of the annual film quota could force the studio to sell its stake in Miramax.
The settlement has drawn some criticism for not going far enough to protect CNN’s editorial independence under CEO David Ellison .
“America is free only when the media is competitive, independent, and accountable to the people,” New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement . “This merger strikes a chilling blow against that freedom — and hands even more power to billionaires like David Ellison to decide what Americans see and hear, all while lifting scrutiny off the federal leaders who pushed it through.”

articles.title_orig: El Niño goes wild: Pacific Ocean under siege from tropical cyclones
articles.title_zh: El Niño goes wild: Pacific Ocean under siege from tropical cyclones
articles.content_orig:
The wild and woolly Pacific basin – fueled by a powerful El Niño – continues to spew forth tropical cyclones of all shapes and sizes. As of the afternoon of Sept. 22, a dangerous Category 5 180-mph hurricane (Hurricane Polo) was threatening the west coast of Mexico and pushing a swath of moisture into New Mexico.
At the same time, a smaller developing system was being watched nervously close to Hawaii.
And to top it off, yet another tropical cyclone, Odalys, could be drawn into a rare meteorological dance in the eastern Pacific with Polo known as the Fujiwhara Effect.
All the action in the Pacific is in contrast to the sleepy Atlantic basin, which has yet to see a single hurricane so far this year. Only six rather unremarkable tropical storms have formed there this season.
Hurricane Polo rapidly intensified into a Category 5 hurricane by the afternoon of Sept. 22 with peak sustained winds of 180 mph and higher gusts as it moves along just off the Mexican coast, according to the National Hurricane Center.
Overall, Polo's maximum sustained winds increased by an incredible 95 mph in 22 hours. (Between 3 p.m. on Sept. 21 and 1 p.m. on Sept. 22).
It's the third Category 5 hurricane in the eastern Pacific during this hurricane season, putting 2026 into a tie with the 1994 season as the most Category 5s on record by Sept. 22, Colorado State University hurricane scientist Phil Klotzbach posted on X .
Still, "despite its great strength, Polo remains a relatively small cyclone with its hurricane and tropical-storm-force winds estimated to only extend about 30 and 80 nautical miles from the eye, respectively," according to a Sept. 22 forecast discussion from the hurricane center.
Otherwise unremarkable Tropical Storm (soon to be hurricane) Odalys could interact with Polo as the storms edge closer together off the coast of Mexico in a few days.
"A stunning scenario would be two major hurricanes side-by-side off the southern tip of Baja California, [while] one (Polo) or the other (Odalys) sling-shots away from the 'binary system,'" n oted Weather Trader meteorologist Ryan Maue on X.
"Fujiwara Effect hurricane or typhoon interactions are highly unpredictable-->climate chaos!," Maue said on X.
The hurricane center mentions this interaction in their forecast discussion of Polo: "The steering currents become more uncertain over the weekend when Polo reaches the western edge of the ridge and nears Tropical Storm Odalys to its west."
And it's also mentioned in the Odalys (pronounced oh-DAL-ess) discussion: "After day three, the uncertainty in the track increases due to potential interaction with Hurricane Polo, which could cause Odalys to slow down late in the forecast period."
When two storms or hurricanes spinning in the same direction pass close enough to each other, they begin an intense dance around their common center known as the Fujiwhara effect , the National Weather Service said.
The effect is thought to occur when storms get about 900 miles apart.
Storms involved in the Fujiwhara effect are rotating around one another as if they had locked arms and were square dancing. Rather than each storm spinning about the other, they are actually moving about a central point between them, as if both were tied to the same post and each swung around it separately of the other.
A good way to picture this is to think of two ice skaters who skate quickly toward each other, nearly on a collision course, grab hands as they are about to pass and spin vigorously around in one big circle with their joined hands at the center.
According to Weather.com, the stronger storm often dominates, tugging the weaker one into its circulation, but in rare cases, two storms of similar strength can combine, creating a single, more powerful storm .
Hawaiian Island residents, who have felt the influence of six tropical storms or hurricanes already this year, are being asked to watch the weather closely yet again as a seventh potential storm could bring rain to the Big Island as early as Sept. 23.
The potential storm is actually the remnants of Tropical Depression Fifteen-E, which dissipated on Sept. 15. The hurricane center indicates environmental conditions are favorable for the remnants to become a tropical depression again, with the chances of storm formation at 70% over 48 hours and 90% over the next seven days.
By Sept. 24, computer forecast models show a potential tropical cyclone drifting toward the Big Island, according to the weather service office in Honolulu. Heavy rains associated with the storm are forecast to spread over the southeastern Hawaiian Islands starting Sept. 23, whether or not it organizes into a named storm, the national weather service said.
While the strength and position of the storm still appear highly uncertain, there’s "a significant potential for a prolonged heavy rain event" over the windward and southeast areas of the Big Island, the weather service warned. A flood watch could be issued later in the week.
Potential wind impacts also remain uncertain, but the weather service indicates a "high likelihood" of at least gusty trade winds of 50 to 60 mph by Sept. 25.
As Hurricane Polo moves along in the Pacific south of Mexico, it's helping to push an intense swath of tropical moisture northward into New Mexico this week, said Bob Oravec, a meteorologist at the weather service's Weather Prediction Center.
"Even though Polo will remain well offshore, some of its higher moisture values are being drawn northward," Oravec said. In general the Albuquerque weather service region is forecast to receive an average of 3 to 4 inches of rain through Friday, with the potential for more than 5 inches in some isolated locations.
Doyle Rice and Dinah Voyles Pulver are national correspondents for USA TODAY with a focus on weather and climate. Reach them at drice@usatoay.com and dpulver@usatoday.com.

articles.title_orig: Ex-Canadian soldier opens fire at synagogue on Yom Kippur, wounds cop in possible antisemitic attack: officials
articles.title_zh: Ex-Canadian soldier opens fire at synagogue on Yom Kippur, wounds cop in possible antisemitic attack: officials
articles.content_orig:
See more of our coverage in your search results.
An ex-Canadian soldier opened fire outside a synagogue during Yom Kippur services and struck a cop before being gunned down by police in a possible antisemitic attack, officials said.
Shotgun-toting Sean Ward, 29, pulled up in his truck and ripped off shots at two cops stationed outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, around 7 p.m. Sunday, according to the CBC .
Ward struck Constable Jeff Smith, who was working security outside the synagogue along with another cop. The two officers returned fire and hit Ward, who died of his injuries Monday night.
Smith remained in critical but stable condition as of Tuesday.
It was not immediately clear if Ward was targeting the synagogue — located about 110 miles east of Toronto — or law enforcement.
Investigators, however, noted that the timing of the shooting on Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement, suggests the attack may have been motivated by antisemitism .
None of the roughly two dozen congregants inside were injured, but bullets peppered surrounding homes, vehicles and the synagogue’s windows.
“There are dozens of bullet holes in the street behind me and some homes have been hit and there are some vehicles with shot out windows, that sort of thing. So it would have been quite the scene,” Belleville Deputy Police Chief Sheri Meeks said.
Worshipers said they immediately realized gunfire was erupting outside and ducked for cover during the intense exchange of about 25 shots, which lasted mere moments.
“I could say, ‘Oh, this is definitely … someone is shooting here,'” Norm Weddum, the leader of Sons of Jacob, who was in attendance for the service, told CBC. “So that’s when we ran back into the auditorium of the synagogue, closed the doors behind us so as to not leave a visible target and we hit the floor.
“Literally everyone went down. I yelled for everyone to get on to the floor and the shots continued for a few more seconds, and then it was basically over.”
Sons of Jacob always requests extra security on Jewish High Holidays due to threat concerns, Weddum noted.
“Thank God that person was there,” he said, referring to Smith.
Authorities are probing a motive in the shooting.
“It’s believed that [Ward] came in a truck and he had a shotgun and he discharged his firearm at a police officer and then that police officer returned fire and then there was a second officer who arrived and then also discharged [their] firearm,” Kristy Denette, a spokesperson for Ontario’s Special Investigations Unit, told reporters.
Ward joined the Canadian Armed Forces in 2017 and served as an infantry soldier before leaving in 2022 as a corporal.
Meeks said antisemitism has “no place” in Belleville — and announced a heightened police presence across the city.
“Let me be very clear: Antisemitism, hate and violence have no place in our community,” she said.
“Every person deserves to feel safe when attending a place of worship, gathering with loved ones, or participating in community life.”
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Belleville Mayor Neil Ellis all condemned the attack.

articles.title_orig: Gable Steveson responds to sexual assault allegations in first statement since knockout loss at UFC 331
articles.title_zh: Gable Steveson responds to sexual assault allegations in first statement since knockout loss at UFC 331
articles.content_orig:
Gable Steveson broke his silence on Tuesday with his first statement after UFC 331
Gable Steveson had a lot to say in his first statement after suffering a devastating knockout loss at UFC 331 this past weekend, but instead of focusing on the loss, it seems he mostly wanted to address sexual assault allegations from his past while he was competing at the University of Minnesota.
On Tuesday, Steveson released a prepared statement discussing his 12-second knockout loss at UFC 331, focused primarily on responding to opponent Sean Sharaf repeatedly calling him a “rapist” in the days leading up to their fight.
In 2019, Steveson was arrested on sexual misconduct charges. He has always maintained his innocence in the case, and the charges were eventually dropped due to “inadequate evidence.” Steveson was released without facing any criminal penalty. Now seven years later, those allegations came to light again after Sharaf repeatedly called Steveson “a rapist” and “loophole” in the leadup to their fight, and the 2020 Olympic gold medalist decided to address the situation as well as his first-ever loss in the UFC.
Read the full statement below:
“This statement is for my family, my friends, my fans and the people who truly know me and know the kind of man I am. I know there are people who will never support me, no matter what I say or do. That’s their choice. But I’m speaking to the people who know me not just as an athlete but as a husband and a father to a young daughter. Prior to and during fight week, an incident from my college years was brought up by my opponent. I believe it was raised to get in my head but it also reopened something that had been addressed years ago. I want to be clear — I did not do anything alleged. I was never charged with a crime and he matter was ultimately dropped by the district attorney. The allegations were not ignored nor brushed aside. They were thoroughly and heavily reviewed as I fully cooperated with law enforcement, including a seprate Title IX review.
“There were no criminal charges, no conviction, and no finding of responsibility against me. The matter was closed and there is no pending legal issue involving me. My own attorney did their own investigation and stated on the record that even if the law was changed, I would have the same outcome, which now speaks for itself.
I understand how serious allegations like this are and I understand that people may hve questions qhen they hear only part of a story. Moving forward, I am going to keep focusing on my wife, my daughter, my family and he work in front of me. To the people who support me, thank you. I know who I am. My family knows who I am. The people who have walked with me through live know who I am. That’s what maters to me and that’s where I’m going to keep my focus.
“As for my opponent, congratulations, you caught me. A mistake on my end was made. It was your night. Just like my wrestling days after my loss, I came bacbk with an undeniable will to win and focus that led me to the top of my sport. The result of Saturday night, I believe, will catapult me to do the same. I will be great and this won’t deny me.”
Steveson has been called the greatest prospect to enter the sport of MMA thanks to his long list of accolades in wrestling, which includes his Olympic gold medal-winning performance at the 2020 games.
Following his knockout loss this past Saturday, Steveson left the octagon in a hurry without offering Sharaf congratulations on his win, although former UFC two-division champion Jon Jones took responsibility for that decision because he wanted his protégé to get immediate medical attention.
