articles.title_orig: Dolly Parton’s Manager Files for Restraining Order Against Fired Nephew, Alleging Ex-Security Head Sent ‘Terrorizing’ Texts and Threatened to ‘Destroy the Entire Brand’
articles.title_zh: Dolly Parton’s Manager Files for Restraining Order Against Fired Nephew, Alleging Ex-Security Head Sent ‘Terrorizing’ Texts and Threatened to ‘Destroy the Entire Brand’
articles.content_orig:
Dolly Parton‘s longtime manager has filed for a restraining order against her nephew, who until being fired a week ago was her head of security, alleging that the family member is engaged in a campaign of coercion, extortion and violent threats that has terrified employees and associates of her management company and trust to the point that they require their own personal security.
The manager, Danny Nozell, representing She’s Alive, LLC (SAL), dismissed Bryan Seaver, who runs Squadron Augmented Protection Services, LLC (SAPS), on Sept. 15, about three weeks after the country superstar’s Aug. 25 death. It was Seaver who announced his aunt’s death to the world in an Instagram video. But an extensive fiiing made by the trust to a Tennessee court late Tuesday afternoon paint a different portrait of Seaver than the reverent one seen in the death announcement video. The legal paperwork alleges that in colorful and sometimes disturbing language, Seaver referred to himself as a mercenary and “killer” and threatened to interfere with Parton’s businesses, including Dollywood, if he did not receive proper payment, in texts sent both before and after her death.
The filing refers to Seaver’s claims of a paramilitary background and says he has dozens of employees who possess military-grade weaponry, and that some employees no longer come to work as a result of the alleged intimidation, while a lawyer who ran some of Parton’s music affairs stopped working for her as a result of the nephew’s ominous language.
The filing from the attorneys for She’s Alive states: “Mr. Seaver began his campaign of threats, intimidation, and coercion a few weeks prior to Ms. Parton’s passing. Those threats continued after her passing, and he aimed them directly at SAL’s personnel, counsel, and business partners. In writing, he vowed to ‘destroy the entire brand,’ threatened to ‘ratfuck every [business party] entity’ that helps operate Dollywood and called himself ‘literally an international arms dealer and mercenary.’ He threatened that ‘[e]veryone needs to be worried about what I might do,”and told Ms. Parton’s entertainment attorney: ‘I’m not an entertainment person. I’m a killer.’ He also threatened to launch a podcast ‘dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships’ unless he was paid.”
Variety has reviewed all four parts of the request for a restraining order and subsequent jury trial, which are filled with lurid quotes and screenshots of angry text messages said to have been sent to Nozell by Seaver.
Seaver did not immediately respond to Variety‘s request for comment after the request for the restraining order went public. Seaver did issue a statement Tuesday to TMZ, which first reported on the restraining order, telling the outlet, “I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer. However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by… I was talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend and he fancies himself a gangster. A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving.”
Seaver says in the alleged texts that he has been turning down media requests, even though “now I’m the biggest social media post in human history,” apparently referring to the death announcement video. Among the alleged text statements Seaver is said to have written to Nozell that are included in the legal paperwork:
“I’m going to destroy the entire brand if you don’t get these [Dollywood business partners] out of our bit. . . . I’m going to go to Billboard Magazine with my shit. Just like you. I’m going to ratfuck every [Dollywood business partner] entity I can possibly conjure.” (The parenthetical additions represent the lawyers’ explanations.)
And: “I’m not an entertainment person. I’m a killer. I sold 27 million $ worth of ammunition and arms to the Haitian Police on day Dolly died. Entertainment is not my game. I have spent my career breaking things and spying on African and Arab leaders. And protecting Dolly.”
In another text, Seaver is seen as allegedly saying: “All I do is warfare . . . Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do . . . “
“I am vengeance for my people for the next 50 years. I have no debt. I only own swords and guns. My children have 3 houses to live in forever. My wife owns everything. All I have is animosity and memory. But I’m going to spend the next times I have on earth ratfucking anyone that has ever betrayed my family.”
“I’m going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It’s going to be great. Or fucking pay me.”
“Her money better be bigger than I can make elsewhere or I’m going to fuck everyone,”
SAL’s request for the restraining order says Seaver’s alleged threats “have already produced the harm they were designed to cause. Ms. Parton’s trusts and estates attorney withdrew after Mr. Seaver targeted her. SAL personnel have resigned; others no longer report to the office because they fear Mr. Seaver and his armed associates. SAL and its related vendors have been forced to retain private security for its personnel —including at their homes. Ordinary operations have given way to an atmosphere of fear.”
“SAL therefore seeks immediate, narrowly tailored relief pending a full hearing on a temporary injunction,” it continues. “Every day without relief gives Mr. Seaver another opportunity to frighten away a trusted employee, counsel, licensee, brand partner, or other essential counterparty. The campaign is ongoing, its consequences are mounting, and SAL should not be required to wait for the next resignation— or the next threat — to obtain protection.”
The documents note that Seaver had worked for his aunt in running her security for about 20 years.
“Mr. Seaver leveraged his family connection and two decades of funding through Ms. Parton as her security provider to increase the size of his personal militia,” the filing says. “Through his security role, Mr. Seaver had virtually unfettered access to the people, routines, vulnerabilities, and commercial affairs surrounding Ms. Parton’s enterprise. He has used his family connections, his access, and that knowledge to target the particular people and institutions SAL most needs… The written record shows a deliberate progression — from threats against a cornerstone brand relationship, to boasts about arms dealing and warfare, to direct intimidation of counsel, and finally to an express pay-me-or-else threat against Ms. Parton’s brand partnerships.”
Specifically, the action alleges, “SAL has lost specialized legal counsel. Ms. Parton’s trusts and estates lawyer withdrew because of Seaver’s threats.” it asks the judge to provide quick action because “the ongoing safety crisis is inherently irreparable. SAL has retained private security not only for the workplace, but for personnel at their homes.” Furthermore, the estate’s lawyers contend, “the threats are escalating rather than abating. In less than three weeks, Seaver progressed from threatening the Dollywood business partner and the brand, to invoking arms dealing and warfare, to announcing long-term vengeance, to driving away counsel, to telling another attorney he was ‘a killer.'”
Seaver is the son of Parton’s sister, Cassie Parton.
The hundreds of millions of dollars Parton left behind were bound to be the source of family disputes, although few could have predicted an escalation this fast and fiery.
There is positive news ahead for Parton’s millions of fans, as her years-in-the-planning museum is set to open in Nashville in early October, and an adjacent hotel bearing her name has already had a soft launch. Later in the year, the stage musical she oversaw dramatizing her life story will open on Broadway.

articles.title_orig: South Korean solar stocks jump as curbs on Chinese sector expected to remain in place
articles.title_zh: 韩国太阳能股大涨，因预计对中国太阳能行业的限制将继续存在
articles.summary_zh: 韩国太阳能公司韩华解决方案（Hanwha Solutions）和OCI控股公司（OCI Holdings）的股价周三上涨超过8%，因为美国对中国太阳能产品的限制在Trump-Xi峰会之前成为焦点。
articles.content_orig:
Shares of South Korean solar companies Hanwha Solutions and OCI Holdings jumped more than 8% on Wednesday, as U.S. restrictions on Chinese solar products came into focus ahead of the Trump-Xi summit.
The two leaders are set to meet in Washington this week, with trade expected to be among the key issues discussed.
Hana Securities said it was highly unlikely that the U.S. would ease restrictions on Chinese solar products as part of the talks, arguing that Washington increasingly views solar as a strategic industry tied to national security.
"If the U.S. were to ease restrictions on Chinese solar products at the U.S.-China summit, it would effectively mean stepping back from efforts to build a domestic supply chain for a strategic national security asset," analyst Yoon Jae-sung said in a note Wednesday.
He named Hanwha Solutions and OCI Holdings as top picks in the sector, citing a low likelihood of an unfavorable outcome from the U.S.-China summit.
Yoon added that any tariff reductions discussed in the talks were expected to focus on non-strategic goods, pointing to Trump's signing of Section 232 measures on polysilicon and its derivatives in August on national security grounds.
Solar has become a strategic asset spanning AI and semiconductor power demand, semiconductor supply chains, defense and space, making efforts to reduce reliance on Chinese supply increasingly important to Washington, he added.
Wednesday's stock moves came hours after Hanwha Solutions' solar unit Qcells welcomed actions by the U.S. Department of Commerce and U.S. Customs and Border Protection to curb what it called the "illegal stockpiling" of imported solar panels, as the Trump administration moves to implement Section 232 tariffs on polysilicon and its derivatives.
Qcells said the measures would help prevent importers from circumventing U.S. trade policy and support domestic solar manufacturing.
"Flooding the U.S. market with large volumes of imported products is a strategy that companies abroad have long used to undermine American manufacturers," Qcells Global CEO Andy Park said in a statement.
Qcells, which describes itself as the largest silicon-based solar manufacturer in the U.S., has invested $2.5 billion to expand its solar manufacturing operations in Georgia, where it produces solar cells and panels.
OCI Holdings also has a significant U.S. presence through its subsidiary OCI Energy, which earlier this month broke ground on new solar facility in Texas.
articles.content_zh:
韩国太阳能公司韩华解决方案（Hanwha Solutions）和OCI控股公司（OCI Holdings）的股价周三上涨超过8%，因为美国对中国太阳能产品的限制在Trump-Xi峰会之前成为焦点。
两位领导人将于本周在华盛顿会晤，预计贸易将是讨论的关键问题之一。
Hana Securities表示，作为谈判的一部分，美国极不可能放松对中国太阳能产品的限制，认为华盛顿越来越将太阳能视为与国家安全相关的战略产业。
分析师Yoon Jae-sung周三在一份报告中表示：“如果美国在美中峰会上放宽对中国太阳能产品的限制，这实际上意味着放弃为战略国家安全资产建立国内供应链的努力。”。
他将韩华解决方案和OCI控股公司列为该行业的首选，理由是美中峰会产生不利结果的可能性很小。
Yoon补充说，会谈中讨论的任何关税削减预计都将集中在非战略商品上，并指出特朗普以国家安全为由于8月签署了关于多晶硅及其衍生物的232条款措施。
他补充说，太阳能已成为跨越人工智能和半导体电力需求、半导体供应链、国防和太空的战略资产，这使得减少对中国供应的依赖对华盛顿来说变得越来越重要。
周三的股票走势发生在韩华解决方案公司的太阳能部门Qcells欢迎美国商务部和美国海关与边境保护局采取行动遏制其所谓的进口太阳能电池板的“非法储存”几小时后，因为特朗普政府正采取行动对多晶硅及其衍生物征收232关税。
Qcells表示，这些措施将有助于防止进口商规避美国的贸易政策，并支持国内太阳能制造业。
Qcells Global首席执行官Andy Park在一份声明中表示：“大量进口产品涌入美国市场是国外公司长期以来用来削弱美国制造商的策略。”。
Qcells自称是美国最大的硅基太阳能制造商，已投资25亿美元扩大其在佐治亚州的太阳能制造业务，在那里生产太阳能电池和面板。
OCI Holdings还通过其子公司OCI Energy在美国拥有重要业务，该子公司本月早些时候在德克萨斯州破土动工建设了新的太阳能设施。

articles.content_orig:
Wall Street’s Nasdaq hits all-time high as AI frenzy gathers pace
Investors shrug off AI safety concerns and Iran war, sending market to a new peak.
Wall Street’s Nasdaq stock exchange has hit an all-time high, shrugging off concerns about AI safety risks, sky-high tech valuations and the energy shock caused by the United States’ war on Iran.
The Nasdaq Composite index, which is dominated by US tech giants such as Nvidia, Apple and Microsoft, rose 0.45 percent on Tuesday, taking its gains to date this year to more than 17 percent.
- list 1 of 4Celebrities at the Pentagon: How unusual was the Paul brothers’ visit?
- list 2 of 4UNGA Day 1: US and Iran hold talks despite Trump’s threat
- list 3 of 4Kamala Harris campaigns with Abdul El-Sayed to unify Democratic voters
- list 4 of 4Iran cancels Baghdad, Muscat flights as US aviation sanctions take effect
The Nasdaq 100, a narrower index that tracks 100 top companies, jumped 0.82 percent.
The S&P 500, the most popular measure of the overall US stock market, closed essentially flat.
Monolithic Power Systems, a Florida-based manufacturer of power circuits, and Canadian e-commerce company Shopify led the gains, surging 8.1 percent and 7.1 percent, respectively.
Micron Technology, one of the world’s top three memory chip makers along with South Korea’s SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, rose 5 percent.
Chip giant Nvidia, the world’s most valuable company, gained 0.7 percent, while Apple edged up 0.2 percent.
Meta Platforms, which soared 11.4 percent on Monday on excitement surrounding its new AI assistant Muse, dropped 0.63 percent.
Major Asian stock markets opened higher on Wednesday, with Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 and South Korea’s Kospi up about 1.4 percent and 0.1 percent, respectively, in morning trading.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index opened lower, falling more than 0.7 percent during the morning trade.
Oil prices were largely flat on Tuesday, after falling more than 3 percent the previous day amid improving oil flows out of the Gulf and hopes of renewed diplomacy between Washington and Tehran.
Futures for Brent crude, the international benchmark, were trading at $99.18 a barrel as of 01:00 GMT.
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday told reporters that US officials held a “very good” meeting with their Iranian counterparts on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, hours after using his address to the session to warn that he could “annihilate” Iran if Tehran did not agree to a deal on the war.
Trump, whose war on Iran is nearing the seven-month mark, said US and Iranian officials would hold another round of talks in the “very near future”.
Jay Goldberg, a senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners in San Francisco, said signs of diplomatic progress between the US and Iran had refocused investor attention on the potential of AI to generate profits after years of multibillion-dollar investments.
“We have been searching for a clear consumer use case to justify the AI spend, and many see Muse as just that product,” Goldberg told Al Jazeera.
“Personally, I think Muse is just a step in the right direction; there will be better products – probably soon – but Muse is one of those things that are so useful they get investors excited about AI prospects again,” Goldberg said.

articles.title_orig: Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran in UN speech as officials from both countries meet on sidelines
articles.title_zh: 特朗普在联合国演讲中威胁要“消灭”伊朗，因为两国官员在场外会面
articles.summary_zh: 特朗普在联合国演讲中威胁要“消灭”伊朗，因为两国官员在场外会面唐纳德·特朗普总统告诉联合国大会，他面临着一个“重大决定”，即是再次打击伊朗还是寻求和平协议。周二，伊朗代表团的一名成员在纽约观看了总统的演讲，他在演讲中表示，如果冲突得不到解决，他可以“消灭”伊斯兰共和国。
articles.content_orig:
Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran in UN speech as officials from both countries meet on sidelines
President Donald Trump has told the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) he faces a "big decision" on whether to strike Iran again or pursue a peace deal.
A single member of Iran's delegation watched on during the president's speech on Tuesday in New York, in which he said he could "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if the conflict went unresolved.
Before a standing-room-only audience, Trump also rejected "global government", vowed to broker peace between Russia and Ukraine and ensure the US wins the artificial intelligence race.
His comments came on a day of high-level diplomacy, which included talks between US and Iranian representatives.
Trump himself has been meeting more than a dozen world leaders as wars in the Middle East and Ukraine test his foreign policy agenda.
He began his UNGA speech by touting his accomplishments on the economy, immigration, the border and tackling violent crime, in remarks that sounded more pitched to voters in November's US midterm elections than the diplomats in Manhattan.
He spent much of his address justifying the war with Iran, which has spiked global oil prices while dragging down his approval ratings since the US and Israel launched the military action in February.
Trump's tone contrasted with remarks earlier by UN Secretary General António Guterres, who warned global divisions were deepening and underscored the "interdependence" of the world's peoples.
The US president argued that the conflict had prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and demonstrated the value of what he described as peace through strength - ultimatums rather than deal-making or compromise.
"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?"
Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections.
The remarks were indicative of his foreign-policy strategy of coercive diplomacy - threatening overwhelming force while keeping negotiations open.
Trump later told reporters that American officials had had a "very productive" three-hour meeting with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the general assembly.
Iran state TV confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had met US Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff.
Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, quoted by state broadcaster IRNA, later said negotiations took part through a Qatari mediator who communicated Tehran's conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts and to US "acts of aggression".
The BBC asked Witkoff how the meetings had gone as he was leaving the UN building and he responded with a thumbs up. Witkoff later confirmed on X that the talks had been held "through the mediators, who shuttled between the two sides throughout the day".
"They successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove constructive and promising," Witkoff said. "The mediators will continue their work."
In his speech, Trump once again predicted his diplomacy would end Russia's war in Ukraine, which has shown little sign of letting up as the two sides trade tit-for-tat missile and drone strikes deep into each other's territory.
"We're working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will get that one done," he said. "It's going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will meet Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov in New York on Wednesday, according to the State Department.
Trump also played down fears about AI, vowing that the US would not surrender its lead to China because of alarmism or what he described as a "globalist scheme" to control the technology.
The US president argued artificial intelligence should instead be known as "super intelligence".
"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful."
On the sidelines of the general assembly on Tuesday, Trump signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to beef up US military presence on the North Atlantic island.
The deal reaffirms the sovereignty of Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, but grants the US broad access to the island's airspace and territory.
Trump has also been meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung and leaders from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman.
This latter meeting, which also involved leaders from other Arab and Islamic countries, "discussed current regional developments and the situation in the Middle East, as well as ways to consolidate security and stability," the UAE's foreign minister said in a statement.
Earlier, Guterres gave his farewell speech as UN secretary general, urging unnamed superpowers to recognise "that their power isn't so super".
"The fault lines in our world are widening," Guterres said, citing geopolitical rivalries, wars, climate change and artificial intelligence.
By contrast, Trump criticised international institutions, accusing the UN of a "far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats who nobody ever elected".
The US president instead emphasised national sovereignty and "unmatched" American military power.
"There is no global government," he said.
He also warned that the US would not allow threats to establish themselves anywhere in the Western hemisphere.
"If necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States," he said.
Trump accused Cuba's communist government of cultivating ties to left-wing groups in the US, including the Communist Party USA, Antifa and the Democratic Socialists of America.
The Cuban delegation also appeared to walk out of the assembly chamber as Trump turned his sights on them, referring to the island as a "failed state".

articles.title_orig: ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Viral Hits Night Ends With a Three-Way Tie for Top of the Leaderboard: See the Scores, Who Went Home
articles.title_zh: ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Viral Hits Night Ends With a Three-Way Tie for Top of the Leaderboard: See the Scores, Who Went Home
articles.content_orig:
[This story contains spoilers for episode three of Dancing With the Stars season 35.]
Dancing With the Stars paid homage to the hottest songs for Viral Hits Night.
Tuesday night, competing couples hit the ballroom to perform numbers inspired by “some of the biggest viral hits and unforgettable moments that have taken the internet by storm,” per ABC. It marks the third episode of season 35; however the second week of competition after last week’s special two-night premiere.
By the end of Viral Hits Night, Giada De Laurentiis and Alan Bersten were eliminated from DWTS season 35.
Celebrities still in the competition are Tatyana Ali, Tyler Cameron, Jenna Dewan, Ezra French, Amber Glenn, Taylor Hanson, Maura Higgins, Ciara Miller, Jackson Olson, Guillermo Rodriguez, Harry Shum Jr., Julia Stiles and Connor Wood.
Last Tuesday during the premiere, the male celebrities performed and Conner Leavitt was eliminated. Wednesday night, the women hit the ballroom, and Sarah Jane Nader became the second celebrity eliminated.
Jenna and Val Chmerkovskiy kicked off Viral Hits Night, cementing the early lead of 21/30 for their Jive to Katseye’s “Animal.” Ciara and Brandon Armstrong trailed closely behind, scoring an 18/30 after they performed a Tango to “No Broke Boys” by Disco Lines and Tinashe.
Ezra and Daniella Karagach went on to tie Jenna and Val’s score, earning three sevens from the judges. They performed a Cha Cha to Flo Rida’s “Low,” leaving the ballroom on their feet in applause.
After Tatyana and Jan Ravnik danced a Foxtrot to Billie Eilish’s “What Was I Made For?,” host Alfonso Ribeiro announced that Viral Hits Night had already received more fan votes than both premieres. However, just before the eliminated couple was announced, Alfonso announced that the number of votes triumphed over that of the season 34 DWTS finale.
Amber and Pasha Pashkov also emerged to tie the top leaderboard score (21/30) for their Tango to “All the Things She Said” by Harrison, an homage to Heated Rivalry, of course. That meant Jenna, Ezra and Amber tied for the top of the leaderboard; Maura trailed with a 19/30. Giada and Guillermo tied for the bottom of the leaderboard, each with a 12/30.
The couple with the lowest combined total of judges’ scores and viewer votes is eliminated at the end of each DWTS episode. Live voting takes place during the East Coast airing of each show and ends shortly after the final performance; that means if you’re a West Coast viewer and want to vote, you must do so between 5 p.m. PT and roughly 6:45 p.m. PT, as voting ends after the final performance.
See the full list of scores for DWTS’ Viral Hits Night below.
Jenna Dewan and Val Chmerkovskiy: 21/30
Ciara Miller and Brandon Armstrong: 18/30
Tyler Cameron and Sharna Burgess: 16/30
Julia Stiles and Ezra Sosa: 16/30

articles.title_zh: 'Extremely dangerous' Hurricane Polo intensifies to rare category 5 storm
articles.content_orig:
'Extremely dangerous' Hurricane Polo intensifies to rare category 5 storm
Hurricane Polo has rapidly intensified off the coast of Mexico to become one of the most powerful storms of the season in the Pacific Ocean.
A Hurricane Hunter aircraft, operated by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), flew into the storm on Tuesday and recorded sustained wind speeds near 180 mph (285 km/h), with stronger gusts.
NOAA's Miami-based National Hurricane Center called the storm "extremely dangerous" and said its intensification over 24 hours was "truly remarkable".
The slow-moving storm is fuelling up on extremely warm waters caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon and is the season's third category 5 storm, the highest level on the Saffir-Simpson scale.
The storm is predicted to skirt the coast of south-western Mexico, but is not expected to make landfall, a warning from NOAA said.
As it slowly drifts northwest, Polo will drive torrential rainfall in parts of Mexico's south-west coast - which could lead to deadly flooding and mudslides, NOAA said.
Rainfall totals of up to 6in (15cm) are forecast, with 8in possible in some areas. Residents have also been warned of large ocean swells and life-threatening surf conditions for the next few days.
"So far, the information we have is that (Polo) will not make a direct landfall on the coast," Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Tuesday, but she warned residents along the Pacific coast to be vigilant. Sheinbaum highlighted the states of Jalisco, Colima and Michoacan as being at risk.
Data from the Hurricane Hunter aircraft indicated that Polo could still strengthen and would likely stay a category 5 storm for the next few days, because of what NOAA called a "very conducive" environment of extremely warm ocean waters feeding the storm.
Scientists monitoring the ocean temperatures say the current El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record.
Daily sea surface temperatures in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific were 3.05C above average on 19 September - exceeding the previous record of 3.02C set during the very strong El Niño of 2015.
Some longer-term measures of El Niño have not yet hit record levels but this is likely to change, with the peak not expected until later this year.
Warmer ocean waters mean storms can pick up more energy, leading to higher wind speeds.
El Niño is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year.
Trade winds that typically blow from east to west across the Pacific Ocean can weaken or even reverse, allowing warm water to spread eastwards.
Heat is then released from the ocean into the atmosphere which can boost global temperatures and drive changes in weather patterns around the world.

articles.title_orig: Chairman Wicker Delivers Senate Floor Speech on China and Xi Jinping
articles.title_zh: Chairman Wicker Delivers Senate Floor Speech on China and Xi Jinping
articles.content_orig:
Washington — Today, U.S. Senator Roger Wicker, R-Miss., Chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, delivered remarks on the floor of the U.S. Senate, outlining the increasing tempo of Chinese aggression.
In his speech, Chairman Wicker addressed the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) support for Iran, religious persecutions, and international coercion. The chairman encouraged President Trump to raise these points of contention during this week’s bilateral summit.
- Chairman Wicker: “The president might inquire about the purposes of China’s massive military build-up, or about China’s clear support for Iran. This summer, it was all over the press that China gave Iran satellite imagery intelligence, and that intelligence led to the death of American troops.”
- Chairman Wicker: “For nearly a decade, Xi Jinping has consigned more than a million Uyghurs to concentration camps in China’s Xinjiang region. I hope our president will take this visit as an opportunity to advocate for the Uyghur people. The fact that they remain in prison by the millions is a grave injustice and a reminder of Xi Jinping’s many human rights abuses.”
- Chairman Wicker: “I know the president intends to discuss trade and artificial intelligence with the Chinese leadership—and rightfully so. Perhaps some progress will be made. But, Mr. President, during every minute of dialogue, our commander-in-chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected, and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America.”
Click here to watch Chairman Wicker’s full remarks.

articles.summary_zh: When Xi Jinping, China’s leader, touches down in Maryland on Wednesday, he will step out into the arms – perhaps a hug, if Donald Trump’s wishes come true – of a US president who has shown China more
articles.content_orig:
When Xi Jinping, China’s leader, touches down in Maryland on Wednesday, he will step out into the arms – perhaps a hug, if Donald Trump’s wishes come true – of a US president who has shown China more bonhomie than any of his recent predecessors.
The meeting between Xi and Trump this week will be the second time that the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies have talked face to face this year. At the previous summit, held in Beijing in May, there was much talk of building a “strategic stability” between the two powers. But there was little by way of concrete outcomes: the countries remain at loggerheads over trade, export controls and geopolitics.
Despite the goodwill built in May, few anticipate any major breakthroughs this week when Xi makes his first state visit to the US since 2015. “Expectations are very low,” said Bonnie Glaser, a managing director at the US thinkthank the German Marshall Fund. “Nobody is using the term ‘deliverables’.”
One area in which Trump and Xi may reach some consensus is on artificial intelligence safety. Tech executives including Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sundar Pichai of Alphabet, Sam Altman of OpenAI, Tim Cook of Apple, Elon Musk of Tesla, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Jensen Huang of Nvidia will reportedly attend a state dinner at the White House on Thursday evening.
In the past few weeks, the US has been beset by worries that AI is progressing too fast, but that the US must strive to defend its lead over China in the frontier technology – and Trump has pushed back hard against calls to slow its development. “We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said recently. “And frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”
On Sunday, Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, concluded talks with the Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng by proposing an AI safety mechanism to be established between Washington and Beijing. The mechanism appears to stop short of a major safety agreement.
Tuesday’s front page of the People’s Daily, the official newspaper of the Chinese communist party (CCP), ran an article saying that the US and China should “make AI a new frontier for China-US cooperation” and “make good use of the intergovernmental dialogue mechanism on AI”.
António Guterres, the UN secretary general, called on the two countries to establish a dialogue on AI similar to the communication between the US and the Soviet Union during the cold war. “Governments with the greatest AI capabilities have the greatest responsibilities to humanity, to establish channels for dialogue, transparency, trust and cooperation,” Guterres said.
Still, China does not agree with US assessments about the grave threat posed by its AI developments. China’s foreign ministry responded to an essay by Dario Amodei, the Anthropic chief executive, that called for Washington to impede Beijing’s progress, by saying “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance”.
China has already taken steps to mandate the labelling of AI-generated content, to restrict the ability of children to use AI companions and, in keeping with the CCP’s desire to keep tight control on all information, to restrict what can be said by chatbots.
China may be more concerned with what it sees as US attempts to limit is growth. Washington has for years restricted China’s ability to buy the most advanced semiconductors needed for AI development, and this year the US banned the sale of Chinese humanoid robots.
Amanda Hsiao, China director at the Eurasia Group, a political risk consultancy, said: “China doesn’t necessarily see the threat in the same way that the US does. There is a lot of distrust that’s in the way of cooperation. The Chinese are inclined to think of every US call for safety standards or calls from companies for pacing the frontier as means of suppressing Chinese development.”
Next on the agenda will be trade. Washington and Beijing struck a temporary truce in the trade war last year at a summit in South Korea. That truce – which included a pause on tariffs, as well as an agreement for Beijing to loosen restrictions on the export of rare earths – will expire in November.
Beijing is hoping for a longer-term commitment to banish tariffs, which pose a threat to China’s export-driven economy. But reports suggest that the US is unwilling to agree to anything that would weaken its future bargaining power.
Glaser, of the German Marshall Fund, said: “The US side views this as leverage over China and ensuring that they can get deliveries of the rare earths and magnets that American companies need.”
China may not feel the need to negotiate, either. Despite the trade war, China’s exports have surged, and it is on track to reach a $1tn trade surplus for the second year running.
One aspect of the relationship that has shifted since May is the issue of Taiwan. After the Beijing summit, Xi secured a major concession from Trump, when he agreed to pause a $14bn package of US arms sales to Taiwan. US presidents have traditionally excluded the issue of arms sales to Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory, from the US-China relationship.
But Trump has described future weapons sales as a “very good negotiating chip”. The US is now reportedly considering delaying further sales until after the Apec and G20 summits later this year, where Trump and Xi are expected to meet again.
Tuesday’s People’s Daily article said that a stable China-US relationship would “bring more peace, prosperity, and progress to the world”. But for all the talk in Beijing of “strategic stability”, Scott Kennedy, a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, notes that “this is not a G2” alliance of the world’s two dominant powers.
“They are finding a way to manage the bilateral relationship, but they are not whatsoever working together as co-stewards of the international order,” Kennedy wrote in a recent commentary.
China is Iran’s biggest oil buyer and trading partner. After Trump launched strikes against Iran in February, China reportedly put pressure on Tehran behind the scenes to come to the negotiating table. It also slashed oil imports by nearly one-quarter in the first six months of the war, limiting global inflation.
Da Wei, a professor of international relations at Tsinghua University, wrote in a recent essay that this reflected “a more confident China” that “did not exploit the difficulties that the United States faced in the war with Iran”. But Beijing has otherwise done little to resolve the crisis in the Middle East, which it sees as being a mess of Trump’s making.
Last month, Bessent announced an “economic D-day” against Iran and its enablers. The US treasury secretary subsequently claimed to have had “very good private discussions” with Chinese officials over ending the country’s economic ties with Iran.
When it comes to Ukraine, Beijing has shown unwavering support for Moscow since Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, launched his full-scale invasion in 2022.
Ali Wyne, senior research and advocacy adviser on the US and China at the International Crisis Group, said: “The contrast between the world’s incumbent power and its principal challenger will be even sharper in Washington than it was in Beijing in May: while the former is mired once more in the Middle East and straining longstanding alliances, the latter is casting itself as a stabilizing counterweight and the leading champion of a more multipolar order.”
The lack of momentum on thorny geopolitical issues, combined with China’s emphasis on maintaining “strategic stability” above all else, means that few expect there to be major breakthroughs at this week’s summit.
Hsiao added: “It is going to be yet another summit that is high on positive vibes and relatively low ambition in terms of substance.”

articles.title_orig: Japan’s Leader Calls on U.N. to Drop ‘Enemy State’ Label
articles.title_zh: Japan’s Leader Calls on U.N. to Drop ‘Enemy State’ Label
articles.content_orig:
Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, has voiced her country’s “consistent support” for the international criminal court (ICC), after Donald Trump urged member states to abandon the body, calling it “out of control”.
In her speech to the UN general assembly in New York on Tuesday, Takaichi said postwar Japan had “emphasised the rule of law in the resolution of all conflicts” – a commitment she said was reflected in its support for multilateral organisations such as the ICC.
Japan’s leader had faced pressure at home to publicly support the ICC, whose president, Tomoko Akane, is Japanese, after failing to come to its defence in response to Trump’s announcement in August that the US would impose sanctions targeting the entire organisation.
On Tuesday, Trump intensified his criticism of the ICC in his speech to the general assembly. “The United States is equally opposed to the out-of-control institution known as the international criminal court,” he said.
“I call on all nations that are members of the ICC to officially resign from this rogue institution immediately.”
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, has called for the ICC to be dismantled “brick by brick”, describing it as an “intolerable threat to US sovereignty”.
Takaichi avoided direct criticism of the US administration in her UN speech as she seeks to keep Washington on side amid rising tensions in the Asia-Pacific, including a commitment to support democratic Taiwan and address Chinese military activity in the South and East China Seas.
Officials in Tokyo are reportedly concerned that Trump could use Taiwan as leverage when he discusses trade with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, in Washington on Thursday.
Washington is legally obliged to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself. Beijing regards the self-governing island as a province and has vowed to “annex” it, including by force if it can’t convince or coerce Taiwan into accepting what it calls “reunification”.
Takaichi’s most recent comments on the ICC come after a cross-party group of MPs in Japan urged her to demand that Trump withdraw the sanctions, announced in response to its decision to issue a warrant for the arrest of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and an ongoing investigation into alleged war crimes by American troops in Afghanistan.
One of the Japanese lawmakers, former defence minister Gen Nakatani, said the UN general assembly was “a place where a country should make its case to the world”, adding: “We want Japan to protect the ICC through the [prime minister’s] address and contacts with other countries.”
Takaichi said on Tuesday that she and Trump had a “candid exchange” about the ICC during discussions on the sidelines of the general assembly.
In the past, Takaichi had drawn criticism for her lukewarm defence of the ICC, having initially described US sanctions as “very unfortunate”. She later said the measures were “incompatible” with Japan’s stance on the work of the court.
Akane, who has led the ICC since 2024, said she would not be intimidated by the threat of sanctions. Speaking soon after the measures were announced in August, she told reporters: “The ICC will never be defeated. Justice will and should prevail, and we will stay true to that belief.”

‘Dancing With the Stars’ Recap: Who Was Eliminated on Viral Hits Night?
- Week 2 of Dancing With the Stars Season 35 featured the contestants dancing to viral hits.
- The couples were dancing for scores from the judges and votes from viewers.
- At the end of the episode, the pair with the lowest combined scores and votes was eliminated.
Week 2 of Dancing With the Stars brought your favorite viral hits to the dance floor! During the two-part Season 35 premiere in Week 1, both new pros Adele Zaikman and Hailey Bills were eliminated with their celebs, Conner Leavitt and Sarah Jane Nader, respectively, but the show went on for the other 14 couples.
Throughout the September 22 episode, the celebs and their pro partners took the ballroom floor to wow the judges with dances to songs that have found popularity on social media, including “All the Things She Said” by Harrison, which went viral after being featured in Heated Rivalry, and “What Was I Made For?” by Billie Eilish, which had everyone in their feels after watching Barbie.
Scroll down for a complete recap of the episode.
Jenna Dewan & Val Chmerkovskiy — 21/30
After Carrie Ann Inaba‘s feedback last week about Jenna Dewan and Val Chmerkovskiy’s teamwork, Dewan was determined to make a splash with a jive to “Animal” by KATSEYE. Bruno Tonioli raved, “What a way to start the show,” calling Dewan “a sexy beast [who] did not miss a beat.”
Inaba explained, “Tonight, what I saw was connected resistance.” She later added, “I’m excited because it was so good.” For Derek Hough‘s one-word response, he shared, “Fast-fierce-fantastic.” (We’re sure the hyphens were in there.)
View this post on Instagram
After their dance, Dewan told Julianne Hough that she really wanted to show Inaba how strong their partnership could be. With 7s from all three judges, Dewan finished with a 21/30.
Ciara Miller & Brandon Armstrong — 18/30
Last week, Ciara Miller got vulnerable on the dance floor, with Inaba declaring that she could “see” her. Ready to work on their frame, Miller and Brandon Armstrong took to the floor with a tango to “No Broke Boys” by Disco Lines and Tinashe.
While Miller’s heel got caught, Inaba cheered, “Ciara has entered the building!” According to Hough, the duo still needs to watch their frame, but he thought that Miller was absolutely radiant. During his one(ish) word statement, Tonioli shared, “Beautiful, my darling.”
View this post on Instagram
With 6s across the board, Miller got 18/30, exclaiming that she was incredibly grateful.
Tyler Cameron & Sharna Burgess — 16/30
Garrett Graham (Belmont Cameli), is that you? For their Week 2 dance, Bachelor Nation’s Tyler Cameron and pro Sharna Burgess danced a salsa to “Girls” by The Kid LAROI, which went viral after the song was featured on Off Campus. Trust us, Cameron’s moves were just as hot as the Briar U hockey star’s.
As Cameron and Burgess teased earlier in the week, his shirt did come off, and the Bachelor star did do the Off Campus fist-to-hips dance move. “You were lifting Sharna up like a He-Man sword,” Hough explained before calling out the content. “It felt more like a cabaret than a salsa.” Tonioli added, “I have to agree with Derek” after calling Cameron a “Terminator.” As Inaba briefly put it, “Agreed, but impressive”
View this post on Instagram
Dedicating their dance to the girls and the gays this week, Cameron received a 6 from Inaba and 5s from the guys, getting a 16/30.
Julia Stiles & Ezra Sosa — 16/30
According to actress Julia Stiles, she is reclaiming her relationship with being open and vulnerable in the public eye by being on Dancing With the Stars. She and Ezra Sosa took on the tango for Week 2 with “The Door” by Teddy Swims.
Tonioli told Stiles, “Some beats were very, very good but at times there were stumbles, and you know that.” Agreeing, Inaba shared, “What’s beautiful about you is your posture… But it’s also working against you.” Derek’s “one” word was “good performance.”
View this post on Instagram
With a 6 from Hough and 5s from Tonioli and Inaba, Stiles received a 16/30 from the judges.
Jackson Olson & Emma Slater — 18/30
After landing a collection of 5s last week, Jackson Olson is “determined” to do better. This week, Emma Slater challenged Olson to his first ballroom dance in frame, a foxtrot to “That’s So True” by Gracie Abrams.
Praised for a “smooth” foxtrot by Alfonso Ribeiro, Olson received rave reviews compared to last week. “Whoa, improvement,” Inaba told Olson. “You settled into it. The partnership is working.” Hough added, “I was really impressed by your frame,” explaining how important it is to maintain that form. For Tonioli’s one word, he told them, “What we all feel — charmed.”
View this post on Instagram
With 6s across the board, Slater was “ecstatic” to see a one-point bump from each judge. Olson received an 18/30.
Giada De Laurentiis & Alan Bersten — 12/30
After surprising everyone, including herself, Giada De Laurentiis hoped to surprise herself again with a salsa (and her first lifts) to “Bella Ciao” by Becky G. Both De Laurentiis and pro Alan Bersten appeared to have a tearful rehearsal process this week that Julianne Hough referred to as “healthy friction.”
Derek Hough pointed out a few missteps during their dance, sharing that De Laurentiis is still a little timid. As Tonioli put it, “You gave me salsa without spice, that is a problem.” He added, “You have to let it go. I can see you thinking.” Unfortunately, Inaba’s word for De Laurentiis was “Shake-y.”
View this post on Instagram
The full panel was booed as they gave 4s across the board. De Laurentiis received a 12/30, which she called “disappointing.”
Connor Wood & Rylee Arnold — 15/30
Content creator Connor Wood hoped to go viral with his tango with Rylee Arnold to “12 to 12” by Sombr. Telling Wood he was going to be brutally honest after the duo made a few noticeable mistakes during their dance, Tonioli explained, “There were a lot of mistakes tonight, and you know that… But the good bits were excellent.”
“That’s such a shame,” Inaba commented, giving multiple compliments before addressing their pitfall. “It’s a mistake, which is why our scores must be what they are.” For his one word, Hough shouted out Wood’s grandmother, with whom he went viral for the first time, saying, “Grandma Mimi.”
View this post on Instagram
Still, Wood received 5s across the board, with a 15/30.
Ezra Frech & Daniella Karagach — 21/30
After coming in third last week, Daniella Karagach challenged Ezra Frech to what she called the most difficult dance: The cha-cha. Together, they took the floor in shades to dance to “Low” by Flo Rida. “This ballroom was torn down tonight,” Ribiero exclaimed after their dance concluded.
“What the frick, Ezra Frech!” Inaba exclaimed, calling their dance “down and dirty,” before adding that the track star “demands excellence from himself.” Recalling his season with Paralympian Amy Purdy, Hough shared, “I am just in awe of you, my friend.”
View this post on Instagram
With 7s from all the judges, Frech received a 21/30.
Tatyana Ali & Jan Ravnik — 18/30
Preparing a foxtrot to “What Was I Made For?” by Billie Eilish with Jan Ravnik, Tatyana Ali looked back at overcoming harsh words from critics in her past. After a misstep through her off her game last week, Ali brought it for Week 2.
“You were absolutely beautiful,” Hough told Ali. “That was breathtaking.” Tonioli commented on the vulnerable dance sharing, “It had such a soft and gentle quality… Beautiful storytelling.” He joked, adding, “The footwork, I assume, was good, but it was lost in the fog.” Inaba’s one word was “touching.”
View this post on Instagram
Ali received 6s across the board, with an 18/30.
Amber Glenn & Pasha Pashkov — 21/30
Making an iconic reference to Heated Rivalry and her personal connection to the series having come out in 2019, Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov danced a tango to “All the Things She Said” by Harrison, who was in the ballroom DJing the song.

articles.title_zh: ‘Dancing With the Stars’ eliminates another couple during ‘Viral Hits Night’
articles.content_orig:
‘Dancing With the Stars’ eliminates another couple during ‘Viral Hits Night’
“Dancing With the Stars” is continuing to whittle down the competition.
Celebrity chef and host Giada De Laurentiis and her pro partner, Alan Bersten, were eliminated at the end of the “Viral Hits Night” episode Tuesday night.
This week’s episode saw the Season 35 cast perform routines “inspired by some of the biggest viral hits and unforgettable moments that have taken the internet by storm,” per an ABC press release.
Prior to the elimination, co-hosts Julianne Hough and Alfonso Ribeiro revealed the other two couples in danger of going home: “Bachelor Nation” star Tyler Cameron (and partner Sharna Burgess) and “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” star Guillermo Rodriguez (and partner Witney Carson).
During Tuesday night’s episode, De Laurentiis landed at the bottom of the leaderboard with a score of 12/30 for their Salsa to Becky G’s “Bella Ciao.”
Three celebrities and their pros found themselves atop the scoreboard by scoring 21/30.
Those competitors included “Step Up” actress Jenna Dewan and partner Val Chmerkovskiy (who performed a Jive to KATSEYE’s “Animal”), Paralympian gold medalist Ezra French and partner Daniella Karagach (who performed a Cha Cha to Flo Rida’s “Low”) and Olympian gold medal-winning figure skater Amber Glenn and partner Pasha Pashkov (who performed a Tango to “All the Things She Said” by Harrison).
Stay one step ahead with all the exclusive tea on your favorite reality TV stars!
Sign up for Virtual Reali-Tea with Danny and Evan, our must-read newsletter!
Following closely behind was “Traitors” alum Maura Higgins and her partner, Mark Ballas, who scored a 19/30 for their Cha Cha to Earth, Wind & Fire’s “September.”
Four pairs also tied with a respectable score of 18/30, including “Summer House” star Ciara Miller and partner Brandon Armstrong (who performed a Tango to “No Broke Boys” by Disco Lines & Tinashe) as well as Savannah Bananas star Jackson Olson and partner Emma Slater (who performed a Foxtrot to “That’s So True” by Gracie Abrams).
Also scoring 18/30 were “The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air” star Tatyana Ali and partner Jan Ravnik (who performed a Foxtrot to Billie Eilish’s “What Was I Made For?”) and “Glee” alum Harry Shum Jr. and partner Jenna Johnson (who performed a Viennese Waltz to “Iris” by the Goo Goo Dolls).
Cameron and Burgess earned a 16/30 for their Salsa to “Girls” by The Kid LAROI, matching the score of “Save the Last Dance” actress Julia Stiles and pro partner Ezra Sosa’s Tango to “The Door.”
Comedian Connor Wood and pro partner Rylee Arnold’s Tango to “12 to 12” by sombr earned them a 15/30, while singer Taylor Hanson and pro partner Britt Stewart’s Cha Cha to DNCE’s “Cake By the Ocean” scored them a 15/30.
Landing at the bottom alongside De Laurentiis was Rodriguez and Carson’s Paso Doble to Rihanna’s “Where Have You Been,” which also scored them a 12/30.
Last week’s two-night premiere saw “Secret Lives of Mormon Wives” star Conner Leavitt and “Love Thy Nader” star Sarah Jane Nader sent packing in back-to-back eliminations.
On the flip side, Shum Jr. and Higgins topped the leaderboard in their respective nights — with the male celebrities performing in the first night of competition and the female celebrities hitting the ballroom during the second night.
New episodes of “DWTS” will air Tuesdays at 8 p.m. ET on ABC and Disney+, and will stream on Hulu the following day.

articles.title_orig: Dancing With the Stars Eliminates 3rd Celebrity After "Shaky" Performance
articles.title_zh: Dancing With the Stars Eliminates 3rd Celebrity After "Shaky" Performance
articles.content_orig:
The dance floor just got a little less crowded.
Dancing With the Stars contestant Giada De Laurentiis was knocked out of the season 35 competition after ranking the lowest alongside ballroom pro Alan Bersten during week two.
In the Sept. 22 episode, the chef danced a tango to “Venus” by Shocking Blue, bringing the evening's "Viral Hits Night" theme to life.
But judge Bruno Tonioli called it a “salsa without spice” and told De Laurentiis she needed to “go for it” like “jumping off a cliff.” Meanwhile, judge Carrie Ann Inaba summed up the performance with one word: "Shaky."
After the judges revealed their scores of 12 out of 30, De Laurentiis noted, "It's disappointing, but hopefully people will vote for us, and I'll get another shot."
"I think I tend to go faster, and I need to learn to slow down," the 56-year-old explained. "That's my lesson to be learned."
After the elimination, she noted, "I tried my best, and it wasn't best enough, but I did try my best."
And the elimination marked the third star to lose their spot in line for the Mirrorball following the ABC hit's two-night premiere, beginning Sept. 15. Secret Lives of Mormon Wives' Conner Leavitt was the first celebrity sent home after a salsa with pro Adele Zaikman didn't bring enough heat to the judges' table opening night.
"Obviously, going home first was not how I wanted to end my Dancing With the Stars experience," Conner, husband of DWTS semi-finalist Whitney Leavitt, explained on TikTok Sept. 17. "But I can genuinely say I had an incredible time. I loved being out there. I loved learning something completely new."
Following his departure, Conner's fellow Hulu realityverse member Sarah Jane Nader was eliminated on night two. The Love Thy Nader personality was partnered with pro Hailey Bills, together becoming the show's third same-sex pairing. (JoJo Siwa and Jenna Johnson, who placed second on season 30, were the first.)
As such, the 24-year-old was proud of how her DWTS run honored her community as a bisexual woman, despite ending sooner than older sister Brooks Nader's ascent to ninth place with her now-ex Gleb Savchenko in 2024.
"As sad as we are to not dance next week—we were so excited—we're just grateful we had this opportunity," Sarah Jane told Good Morning America after the results. "Our partnership was so special. Not only because we became best friends, but because we represent a whole community."
But the 2026 competition is still anyone's game. Read on to see all of the stars still waltzing in for the win.

articles.title_orig: Trump Threatens Annihilation in Iran in UN Speech and Lays Out Winner-Takes-All Vision
articles.title_zh: Trump Threatens Annihilation in Iran in UN Speech and Lays Out Winner-Takes-All Vision
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump made multiple false claims in his address to the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, though he largely stuck to a prepared text.
Here is a fact check of some of his assertions.
Trump, repeating a frequent false claim, said, “Since I took office, it has been my great honor to settle eight wars.”
He specified that he was talking about conflicts between Cambodia and Thailand; Kosovo and Serbia; Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo; India and Pakistan; Armenia and Azerbaijan; and the war in Gaza. And he has previously claimed that the other two wars he ended were last year’s brief conflict between Israel and Iran and a supposed war between Egypt and Ethiopia.
Trump’s “eight” figure is a clear exaggeration.
His list includes two situations that were never actually wars during his tenure. The situation between Egypt and Ethiopia was a diplomatic dispute over an Ethiopian dam project, not a war, and the mysterious supposed issue he says he resolved between Serbia and Kosovo was also not a war.
In addition, the war involving Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo has not ended despite a peace agreement brokered by the Trump administration. And though Trump cited the war in Gaza, Israel continues to conduct frequent attacks in the enclave despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreement.
Trump did help to end the brief 2025 conflict between Israel and Iran, though Israel proceeded to join the US in starting another war against Iran in 2026.
Trump scoffed at dire warnings that artificial intelligence might eventually attack or kill people, claiming they are coming from “the very same people who said we’ll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming, a name since reborn to climate change because the planet was cooling, not warming, and nobody was dead.”
There are at least four things wrong with his sentence about global warming.
First, the phrase “global warming” remains in widespread use even though the phrase “climate change” is also common; they mean different things. Climate scientists use both, often saying “global warming” when referring to the long-term trend of increasing global temperature and “climate change” when referring to the numerous effects the world is experiencing because of that trend. (NASA, part of the Trump-led federal government, explains the difference between the terms on its website.) For example, a 2023 report from the UN’s climate change panel is titled “Climate Change 2023: Synthesis Report,” but it says this: “Human activities, principally through emissions of greenhouse gases, have unequivocally caused global warming, with global surface temperature reaching 1.1°C above 1850-1900 in 2011-2020.”
Second, while Trump didn’t say what time period he was talking about, he didn’t acknowledge that the world has continued to get warmer, not cooler. The UN’s World Meteorological Organization reported in January that “the past 11 years have been the 11 warmest on record,” with 2023, 2024 and 2025 the three very warmest — as NASA also found — though 2025 wasn’t as hot as 2024.
Third, experts widely disagree that “nobody” has died from the various impacts of a warming world. It’s impossible to pinpoint a precise death number, but some estimates total in the millions. The deaths are likely to continue; the World Health Organization says, “Between 2030 and 2050, climate change is expected to cause approximately 250,000 additional deaths per year, from undernutrition, malaria, diarrhea and heat stress alone.”
Fourth, while somebody somewhere might have said that “we’ll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming,” that isn’t how an expert report framed the issue.
A widely discussed 2018 report from climate scientists said the world needed to sharply cut carbon emissions within the next 12 years to be on track to limit warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels; scientists said above that threshold, the potential deadly impacts from climate change would be larger. Though the 2018 report was often oversimplified by politicians, the expert claim was never that “we’ll all be dead in 12 years” — it was that significant action was needed within 12 years to improve the future. (The UN program reported earlier this month that the world is set to exceed the 1.5-degree increase, “likely within the next few years.”)
Trump delivered a more cautious version of his inaccurate previous boast that $21 trillion in investment is pouring into the US, this time saying, “We’ve secured commitments for $21 trillion in new investments from all over the planet.” His figure has no apparent basis even with the “secured commitments for” caveat; the White House has never been able to substantiate it.
When the president spoke at the UN, the White House’s own website claimed there had been “$11.2 trillion” in “major investment announcements” during Trump’s second term, far less than the “$21 trillion” in commitments the president cited. And a detailed CNN review in 2025 found the White House list was counting trillions in vague investment pledges, pledges that were about “bilateral trade” or “economic exchange” rather than investment in the US, and vague statements that didn’t even rise to the level of pledges.
The White House figure includes pledges from US-based companies as well as foreign entities. Federal data shows that new foreign direct investment in the US was about $232 billion in 2025.
Trump defended the Iran war at length. And he claimed, “The cowards and traitors would love to say the United States is low on munitions, but that’s not true. We have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using, and we’re building them at levels that we have never done before.”
We don’t have access to classified information on the precise current state of US munitions stockpiles, and it’s not clear who Trump is calling “cowards and traitors.” But it’s not just CNN and other media outlets that have reported that the war with Iran has depleted at least some US munitions levels; the federal inspector general overseeing the Defense Department and the nonpartisan federal Congressional Budget Office essentially said the same in separate reports released last week.
The inspector general report, which discussed the period from the beginning of April through the end of June, said a Defense Department acquisitions office “said that the munitions expenditure in (the war) has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply.”
The report said the acquisitions office also noted that while the Pentagon “has begun to implement mitigation strategies, the defense industrial base requires ‘significant lead time’ to expand production capacities.” The report specified: “The most persistent bottlenecks remain in the production of solid rocket motors, the availability of high-grade explosives and propellants, and the recruitment of skilled manufacturing labor.”
The Congressional Budget Office report said there is a “shortfall” of missile defense interceptors and that the war will leave “the United States with a reduced inventory of interceptors for several years.” The report said the Defense Department had a “limited” inventory of interceptors even before Israel and the US attacked Iran during a brief conflict in June 2025, and that the budget office’s research indicates the US “has probably used between one-half and two-thirds of its inventory of those munitions since June 2025.”
“Given the number of missile defense interceptors that DoD has recently used, their currently low production rates, and the historical difficulty of scaling up their production, rebuilding DoD’s inventory of interceptors would probably take at least five years — even if production was increased,” the report said.
The Defense Department has consistently said it’s not true that there are any munitions shortfalls, and it did so again last week.

articles.title_orig: Ella Langley says 'Choosin' Texas' success is 'changing my life' after her song breaks Mariah Carey's record
articles.title_zh: Ella Langley says 'Choosin' Texas' success is 'changing my life' after her song breaks Mariah Carey's record
articles.content_orig:
Ella Langley knew "Choosin' Texas" was special. Even she couldn't have predicted just how far it would go.
On Tuesday night, Langley took to Instagram to celebrate making Billboard Hot 100 history this week when "Choosin' Texas" logged its 23rd week at No. 1, surpassing Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You" for the longest reign at the top of the chart.
"I'm genuinely trying to find the words to explain what's going on in my brain today," Langley began her video. "What? I don't know. Thank you so much. Thank you for loving this song, for listening to it. I feel like… I just don't even know what to say at this point. I'm running out of hyperboles to describe how I feel, so I will just let my dog in the background show you his excitement," she continued as her dog barked.
"Just thank you. Thank you so much. It's changing my life. It's changing the lives of the writers of this song. It's changing the lives of my family and it is truly growing an atmosphere for something I'm gonna be able to do the rest of my life and I just… today doesn't feel like a real thing," Langley said. "It feels fake and somebody's going to come in and be like 'haha we're kidding the whole time just kidding.'"
ELLA LANGLEY SEEMINGLY FIRES BACK AFTER DOJA CAT'S BRUTAL TAKE ON HER CHART-TOPPING HIT
"I'm really excited to just experience a moment like this in my life," she said.
The country music star told her fans that she was going to celebrate tonight before ending with, "Choosin' T… that's the one huh?"
In a resurfaced interview with Billboard from March, when the song was still climbing, Langley admitted its success had already surpassed anything she imagined when she wrote it.
"When we wrote it, I knew it was going on the record. I honestly knew it was going to be the lead single," Langley told Billboard.
"And we love that song, but I don't think I could have ever imagined what's happening with it right now," she continued. "Like I said, every day I wake up and it's doing something that I didn't even know was a goal that I could have had."
"It's just nuts," Langley added. "It's crazy to see the ownership that the fans have taken over it. And the different demographics of people listening to the song is so cool."
What seemed unimaginable to Langley in March has since become historic.
ELLA LANGLEY'S 'CHOOSIN' TEXAS' SPENDS 15 WEEKS AT NUMBER ONE ON THE BILLBOARD HOT 100
"Choosin' Texas" first entered the Hot 100 in November 2025, became Langley's first top 10 in January and reached No. 1 for the first time in February.
The song has also spent 41 weeks at No. 1 on Billboard's Hot Country Songs chart.
Long before it became a record breaker, however, "Choosin' Texas" began with a story about a kangaroo.
Langley recalled writing the song during her first songwriting retreat with country superstar Miranda Lambert and two other writers.
"So, I was on a writer's retreat with Miranda," Langley explained in the resurfaced Billboard interview. "This is our first time that we had written together and obviously we were there with two others."
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Billboard credits Langley, Lambert, Luke Dick and Joybeth Taylor as the four co-writers of "Choosin' Texas."
Langley said Lambert began telling her a story about a pet kangaroo.
"I learned at a young age she had a pet kangaroo and I wanted to ask her about it," Langley recalled. "So, I was like, 'Tell me about this kangaroo that you had. I need to know.'"
ELLA LANGLEY'S TEXAS PHOTO DUMP SENDS COUNTRY MUSIC FANS INTO A FRENZY ONLINE ON INSTAGRAM
Lambert told the group about once being pulled over with the kangaroo riding in the passenger seat and a dog in the back.
"She said she got pulled over and the kangaroo ended up getting her out of a ticket, but she's like, 'Of course, I had Texas plates on, too,'" Langley recalled.
ELLA LANGLEY JOINS MUSIC ROYALTY WITH 'INSANE' MILESTONE FOR 'CHOOSIN' TEXAS'
That was enough to spark the song.
"And I went, 'Well, she's from Texas, I can tell,'" Langley said. "And just from that phrase, it kind of all hit us."
According to Langley, the melody came almost immediately, with Lambert helping develop the story behind it.
"And 45 minutes later, we had that song written," Langley said. "And it was just, it was such a cool experience."
Lambert's involvement didn't end in the writing room.
Langley told Billboard that the country superstar was executive producing her next record and had become someone she could turn to for advice.
"There's not a rulebook to this job," Langley said. "So to be able to have someone like her to ask questions and think, you know, is it, should I be doing this? She's like, 'Hell yeah, you should be doing this.'"
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Even Lambert was surprised by what was happening with "Choosin' Texas."
"My team's calling me every day freaking out about this song," Langley recalled Lambert telling her.
At the time of the March interview, the song had reached No. 5 on the Hot 100.
"How crazy is that?" Langley said.
"And for me, like, what, me? You mean me?"
Six months later, "Choosin' Texas" stands alone as the longest-running No. 1 song in Hot 100 history.
Langley's historic week comes as she continues performing across the country.

The singer recently shared photos from stops in Oxford, Mississippi; Athens, Georgia; and Jacksonville, Florida.
"Oxford, Athens & Jacksonville ❤️," she captioned the Instagram post.
The images showed Langley performing with her guitar, posing near an Ole Miss sign in a dress and red boots, holding a snake and preparing backstage in front of a lighted mirror. Another captured an older couple dancing during her show.
Fans celebrated her record in the comments.
"Congrats @ellalangleymusic on passing Mariah!" one person wrote.

articles.title_orig: Trump backs ban on diesel exports
articles.title_zh: 特朗普支持禁止柴油出口
articles.summary_zh: 特朗普称支持禁止柴油出口，美国柴油均价已飙升至每加仑6.52美元的创纪录水平，同比上涨77%。
articles.content_orig:
President Trump said Tuesday that he would support banning exports of diesel fuel.
"I've said let's not send out the diesel," the president said on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. "We make a lot of diesel. It could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline because when you do that, you know, it's a sort of a flow. It's a balance."
Trump added, "But no, I've called for it. I've called for it within my people. I've been talking about it."
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he's examining whether a diesel export ban is feasible, given overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work.
The national average price of diesel fuel has surged to an all-time record of $6.52 per gallon, according to AAA, a staggering 77% increase compared to this time last year.
Driven primarily by global supply crunches from the wars in Iran and Ukraine, the sudden spike is acting as a massive tax on the US supply chain, which is heavily reliant on diesel to move goods. Because diesel is the economy's primary industrial fuel, its high cost is spilling over into consumer prices nationwide.
Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy, posted on X, "this will backfire and is not good."
"U.S. diesel prices are determined not by a U.S. supply and demand balance, but a global one," De Haan wrote. "Keeping distillates and diesel [at] home does not change the world price that reference our prices. You can't fence off a globally traded commodity by executive order and expect the global price to stop applying to it."
Economist Joseph Brusuelas warned that the export ban could backfire for another reason: if energy producers pull back on production. The US produces 5.3 million barrels per day, above the 3.6 million barrels of daily domestic demand. He says an export ban would create a short-term domestic surplus, which would then have to be sold at a discount. That, in turn, could cause energy firms to pull back on production, sending prices back up.
Jennifer Schonberger is a veteran financial journalist covering markets, the economy, and investing. At Yahoo Finance, she covers the Federal Reserve, Congress, the White House, the Treasury, the SEC, the economy, cryptocurrencies, and the intersection of Washington policy with finance. Follow her on X @Jenniferisms and on Instagram.

articles.content_zh:
特朗普总统周二表示，他将支持禁止柴油燃料出口。
“我说过，别把柴油送出去。”总统在联合国大会场边说。“我们生产大量柴油。这可能会对普通汽车汽油产生一点影响，因为你知道，这是一种流动，是一种平衡。”
特朗普补充说：“不过，是的，我已经呼吁过。我在自己人中间呼吁过。我一直在谈这件事。”
财政部长斯科特·贝森特表示，他正在研究柴油出口禁令是否可行，包括整体炼油产能，以及全面还是部分禁令有效。
据AAA数据，美国柴油平均价格已飙升至每加仑6.52美元的史上最高纪录，与去年同期相比惊人地上涨了77%。
主要由伊朗和乌克兰战争造成的全球供应紧张推动，这一突然飙升正对美国供应链造成沉重打击——美国供应链严重依赖柴油运输货物。由于柴油是经济的主要工业燃料，其高成本正在向全国消费者价格蔓延。
GasBuddy石油分析主管帕特里克·德哈恩在X上发文称，“这会适得其反，并不好”。
“美国柴油价格不是由美国的供需平衡决定的，而是由全球供需决定的。”德哈恩写道。“把馏分油和柴油留在国内并不会改变决定我们价格的全球价格。你不能用行政命令围住一种全球交易的商品，却指望全球价格不再适用于它。”
经济学家约瑟夫·布鲁苏拉斯警告说，出口禁令可能因另一个原因适得其反：如果能源生产商缩减产量。美国日产量530万桶，高于360万桶的国内日需求量。他说，出口禁令会造成短期国内过剩，届时必须折价出售。这反过来可能导致能源公司缩减产量，推高价格。

Editor’s Note: After publication of this story, the official X account of CASI shared a statement “that Air University has decided to close the China Aerospace Studies Institute,” despite the Air Force’s previous statement on the status of the organization. Breaking Defense has requested clarification from the service and will update this story with more information.
WASHINGTON — The Air Force is eliminating civilian staff roles for a service-run organization dedicated to studying Chinese airpower, but is not closing shop on the research entity, according to an Air Force spokesperson.
In a statement to Breaking Defense, the spokesperson said that in response to “an ongoing civilian restructure within” the Air Force’s Air Education and Training Command, civilian staff “will no longer be assigned to China Aerospace Studies Institute (CASI).” The spokesperson added that CASI’s “mission continues” and will be executed by “leveraging assigned military service members to accomplish its objectives.”
Affected civilian employees “will continue in their current positions until further notice and will be evaluated for reassignment,” the spokesperson said.
CASI is a premiere, government-run think tank that regularly publishes research on Beijing’s air and space forces. The entity shares its findings within the US military and the broader defense community to promote understanding of China’s military prowess, with the goal of shaping policy and strategy.
The organization’s most recent work was published Monday. The paper, entitled From Vision to Vigilance: How Beijing’s Space-Science Roadmap Builds a Real-Time Kill Webb, explores how technologies ostensibly geared toward space exploration could instead “support persistent, multi-spectral coverage across the Pacific with near-real time refresh,” the paper’s introduction reads. Those technologies could then be used for military purposes to aid what defense officials call a “kill web,” essentially a network of integrated sensors that can provide multiple ways to track and strike a target.
Trouble at CASI first surfaced on Monday when a civilian staffer posted online about roles being eliminated, including a claim that the Air Force planned to “shutter” the institute. The move, coming the week that Chinese President Xi Jinping is slated to visit the United States, prompted questions about similar study projects run by the Army and Navy.

articles.title_orig: China launches commercial radio-tracking satellites in electronic warfare leap
articles.title_zh: 中国发射商业无线电跟踪卫星实现电子战飞跃
articles.summary_zh: 中国发射首颗商用无线电跟踪卫星实现电子战飞跃
articles.content_orig:
China launches its first commercial radio-tracking satellites in electronic warfare leap
The trio of satellites, named after an all-hearing mythical beast, can track enemy warships, hidden radars and electronic jammers
China has just taken a quiet but critical step in space-based electronic warfare.
A Lijian-1 Y18 rocket lifted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in northern China at noon on Sunday, carrying nine satellites. Among them were three Diting-01 satellites, which successfully entered their planned orbit.
The trio is named after Diting, a beast from Chinese mythology that crouches beneath the desk of Ksitigarbha, the bodhisattva of the underworld, and can identify all things simply by listening.
The name perfectly captures what these satellites are designed to do.
articles.content_zh:
中国发射首颗商用无线电跟踪卫星实现电子战飞跃
这三颗卫星以一种全听力神话中的野兽命名，可以追踪敌方军舰、隐藏雷达和电子干扰器
中国刚刚在天基电子战方面迈出了一个安静但关键的一步。
周日中午，一枚李剑一号Y18火箭从中国北方酒泉卫星发射中心发射升空，携带9颗卫星。其中包括三颗Diting-01卫星，它们成功进入了计划轨道。
这三人组以中国神话中的野兽地丁命名，地丁蹲在地藏菩萨的桌子下，只需倾听就能识别一切。
这个名字完美地捕捉到了这些卫星的设计目的。
